'I\'m the CEO and I need this now' or 'I\'m from IT security, I need your password to fix your access.' Training: verify identity via official channels regardless of claimed authority. No legitimate IT staff will request passwords." }, { q: "Pretexting involves:", opts: ["A. Sending deceptive emails", "B. Creating a fabricated scenario and false identity to manipulate a target into compliance", "C. Following someone through a secure door", "D. Installing keyloggers"], answer: "B", explain: "Pretexting: attacker creates a believable false identity and scenario ('I\'m from IT, we\'re auditing accounts, I need to verify your credentials'). The pretext establishes trust before the malicious request. Defence: verify all identity claims through official channels, never provide credentials over the phone." }, { q: "Clean desk policy mitigates:", opts: ["A. Hard drive failure", "B. Shoulder surfing, document theft, and photography of sensitive information", "C. Network-based data exfiltration", "D. Malware propagation"], answer: "B", explain: "Clean desk: clear sensitive documents, printed materials, and removable media at end of day. Lock screen when leaving. Mitigates: cleaners/visitors seeing sensitive info, theft of printed documents, post-it notes with passwords, photography of confidential data displayed on screen." }, { q: "Typosquatting registers:", opts: ["A. Expired domains from competitors", "B. Visually similar domains (paypa1.com, gooogle.com) to capture mistyped traffic", "C. Subdomains of legitimate sites", "D. The exact same domain on a different TLD"], answer: "B", explain: "Typosquatting: register domains that look like popular sites — swap letters, add/remove letters, use lookalike characters (zero for O, 1 for l). Users mistype URL or click crafted link and land on attacker\'s site. Used for credential harvesting, malware delivery." }, { q: "SPF email record purpose:", opts: ["A. Encrypts email in transit", "B. Lists authorised mail servers for a domain — enables receivers to reject mail from unauthorised senders", "C. Signs email content cryptographically", "D. Controls who can receive emails from a domain"], answer: "B", explain: "SPF: TXT record listing IP addresses and servers authorised to send email for the domain. Receiving mail servers check if the sending IP is in the SPF record. If not: SPF fail. Combined with DMARC p=reject, unauthorised senders are blocked." } ] }, { id: "11-39", week: 11, day: 39, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Data Privacy, Protection & Secure Destruction", objective: "Understand data classification, DLP, data lifecycle, secure destruction methods, and privacy regulations.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 5.2 Data Privacy", notes: `## Data Classification\n\n**Government:** Top Secret → Secret → Confidential → Unclassified\n**Corporate:** Restricted/Confidential → Internal → Public\n\n---\n\n## Data Types\n\n- **PII:** Personally Identifiable Information (name, SSN, email, biometrics)\n- **PHI:** Protected Health Information (HIPAA) — medical records, diagnoses\n- **PCI data:** Card numbers, CVV, expiry dates\n- **IP:** Trade secrets, source code, patents\n\n---\n\n## Data States\n\n**At rest:** On disk/database. Protect: AES-256 full disk, database encryption.\n**In transit:** Moving over network. Protect: TLS, HTTPS, VPN, SFTP.\n**In use:** In memory. Protect: Trusted Execution Environments, app controls.\n\n---\n\n## DLP (Data Loss Prevention)\n\nDetects and prevents unauthorised data exfiltration.\n\n- **Endpoint DLP:** Blocks USB copy, printing, email of PII.\n- **Network DLP:** Inspects outbound traffic for sensitive patterns.\n- **Cloud DLP:** Monitors cloud storage (AWS Macie, Google DLP).\n\nDetection methods: regex patterns (SSN), document fingerprinting, ML classification.\n\n---\n\n## Secure Data Destruction\n\n| Method | Best For | Security Level |\n|--------|----------|----------------|\n| Shredding | Paper, optical media | High |\n| Degaussing | Magnetic drives (HDD, tape) | High |\n| Physical destruction | All media types | Highest |\n| Cryptographic erasure | Encrypted drives | High |\n| Secure erase (vendor cmd) | SSDs | High |\n\nSimple deletion: insufficient — data recoverable from unallocated space with free tools.\nDegaussing does NOT work on SSDs (not magnetic).\n\n---\n\n## Privacy Concepts\n\n**Data minimisation:** Collect only what you need.\n**Purpose limitation:** Use data only for the stated purpose.\n**Right to erasure (GDPR):** Delete on request if no legitimate retention purpose.\n**Anonymisation:** Irreversible removal of identifiers. Not personal data.\n**Pseudonymisation:** Replace identifiers with tokens — can re-identify with key. GDPR still applies.\n**Privacy by design:** Build privacy in from the start — not bolted on.`, exercise: { title: "Data Protection Scenarios", instructions: "Apply the correct data protection control or concept.", items: [ "Company stores credit card numbers hashed with MD5. Why is this inappropriate?", "Employee copies 50,000 customer records to personal USB. What control prevents this?", "Decommissioned server hard drive is deleted and the server donated. What risk remains?", "User requests GDPR erasure. Company has 7-year financial retention requirement. How to balance?", "Anonymisation vs pseudonymisation — which still falls under GDPR?", "Stolen unencrypted laptop with customer data. GDPR obligation?", "Why is data minimisation both a privacy AND security best practice?", "When is cryptographic erasure particularly useful compared to physical destruction?" ], answer: `1. Hashing is one-way — you cannot recover the card number for payment processing. For card storage: use reversible AES-256 encryption (PCI DSS Req 3.4). Additionally: PCI DSS PROHIBITS storing CVV/CVC at all, regardless of encryption method. 2. Endpoint DLP. Detects and blocks copying files containing PII patterns to removable media. Can also block: emailing sensitive files externally, printing, uploading to cloud storage. The DLP policy triggers on detected sensitive content. 3. Simple deletion leaves data in unallocated disk space — recoverable with free forensic tools. Correct disposal: degaussing (HDD), secure erase command (SSD), or physical destruction. Obtain a certificate of destruction from the disposal vendor. 4. Partial erasure. Financial transaction records may be retained 7 years under tax law (legitimate purpose exception). Delete: marketing data, preferences, non-financial personal data. Inform the user which data was retained and the legal basis. Document in internal deletion records. 5. Pseudonymisation still falls under GDPR — data can be re-identified using the key table. True anonymisation (irreversible) falls outside GDPR scope. Achieving true anonymisation is very difficult in practice — most "anonymous" datasets can be re-identified via combination of attributes. 6. Notify supervisory authority (e.g. UK ICO) within 72 hours (GDPR Art 33). Assess whether individuals need notification (Art 34 — if high risk). Document in breach register. Full disk encryption would have meant no breach to report — encrypted stolen data is just encrypted data, no personal data exposure. 7. Data minimisation: if you don't collect it, you can't breach it. Smaller data footprint = smaller breach scope, smaller fine, smaller reputational damage. Privacy: GDPR Article 5 compliance. Security: every stored data item is a liability that must be protected. 8. Cryptographic erasure is preferred for: cloud storage (cannot physically destroy provider hardware), SSDs (wear leveling makes overwriting unreliable), large-scale disposal (too many drives for physical destruction). Encrypt all data, destroy the key — mathematically unrecoverable.` }, practical: { title: "Data Protection Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Encrypt sensitive data at rest and securely delete originals", command: `echo "Sensitive: SSN 123-45-6789, Card 4111111111111111" > /tmp/sensitive.txt echo "=== ENCRYPT (AES-256) ===" openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in /tmp/sensitive.txt -out /tmp/sensitive.enc -pass pass:SecureKey123! echo "Encrypted file size: $(wc -c < /tmp/sensitive.enc) bytes" echo -e "\n=== VERIFY UNREADABLE ===" xxd /tmp/sensitive.enc | head -3 echo -e "\n=== DECRYPT AND VERIFY ===" openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -d -in /tmp/sensitive.enc -out /tmp/decrypted.txt -pass pass:SecureKey123! cat /tmp/decrypted.txt echo -e "\n=== SECURE DELETE ORIGINAL ===" shred -vuz /tmp/sensitive.txt 2>&1 | head -3 echo "Original securely overwritten and deleted"`, explain: "AES-256-CBC encrypts the data. The encrypted file is unreadable without the key. shred overwrites the file multiple times before deletion — unlike rm which only removes the directory entry, leaving data recoverable. In production: use full-disk encryption (BitLocker/LUKS) so all data at rest is automatically protected." }, { instruction: "Simulate DLP pattern detection", command: `python3 << 'EOF' import re patterns = { "US SSN": r'\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b', "Credit Card": r'\b4[0-9]{12}(?:[0-9]{3})?\b', "Email": r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b', } docs = { "Safe": "Q3 report attached. Meeting at 2pm.", "Risky": "Patient SSN: 123-45-6789, card 4111111111111111, contact alice@hospital.com", } print("DLP INSPECTION RESULTS") print("=" * 45) for name, text in docs.items(): findings = [] for pat_name, pat in patterns.items(): if re.search(pat, text): findings.append(pat_name) status = "BLOCKED" if findings else "ALLOWED" print(f" {name}: {status} {('— Found: ' + ', '.join(findings)) if findings else ''}") EOF`, explain: "DLP uses regex to detect sensitive data types in content. This is exactly how network and endpoint DLP works — scan outbound content for SSN, card number, NHS number patterns and enforce policies. Production DLP also uses document fingerprinting and ML for context-aware detection." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "Data at rest is protected by:", opts: ["A. TLS and HTTPS", "B. Full disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS), database encryption", "C. VPN tunnels", "D. Firewall ACLs"], answer: "B", explain: "Data at rest: stored on disk/DB. Protect with encryption at the storage layer — BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (macOS), LUKS (Linux), TDE (database). TLS/VPN protect data in transit over networks." }, { q: "Simple file deletion is insufficient because:", opts: ["A. Recycle bin still holds it", "B. Data remains in unallocated disk space — recoverable with free forensic tools", "C. OS keeps cached copy", "D. File system index still references it"], answer: "B", explain: "File deletion: removes directory entry, marks space available — does NOT overwrite data. Forensic tools (Recuver, Autopsy) recover deleted files from unallocated space. Secure methods: shred (overwrite), degauss (HDD), physical destruction, cryptographic erasure (destroy key)." }, { q: "Degaussing is effective for:", opts: ["A. SSDs and flash storage", "B. Magnetic media only — HDDs and tape drives", "C. All storage media equally", "D. Optical discs (CDs/DVDs)"], answer: "B", explain: "Degaussing: strong magnetic field destroys magnetic media. Only works on MAGNETIC storage: HDD, tape. SSDs use flash memory (not magnetic) — degaussing has NO effect. For SSDs: use manufacturer secure erase command or physical destruction." }, { q: "Pseudonymisation under GDPR:", opts: ["A. Falls outside GDPR scope", "B. Is still personal data — re-identification possible with key table, GDPR applies", "C. Requires no security controls", "D. Is equivalent to anonymisation"], answer: "B", explain: "Pseudonymisation: tokens replace identifiers, key table allows re-identification. STILL personal data under GDPR. True anonymisation (irreversible) falls outside GDPR — but is very difficult to achieve. Even 'anonymous' datasets can often be re-identified." }, { q: "DLP (Data Loss Prevention) primary purpose:", opts: ["A. Prevent external network attacks", "B. Detect and prevent unauthorised exfiltration of sensitive data", "C. Manage user access rights", "D. Monitor network bandwidth"], answer: "B", explain: "DLP: monitors content for sensitive data patterns (PII, card numbers, IP) and enforces policies. Blocks: USB copy of PII, emailing sensitive files externally, cloud upload, printing. Endpoint, network, and cloud deployment layers." }, { q: "GDPR right to erasure requires:", opts: ["A. Immediate deletion of all data on any request", "B. Deletion when no legitimate purpose exists — legal retention obligations are exceptions", "C. Deletion within 24 hours", "D. Only deletion of inaccurate data"], answer: "B", explain: "Right to erasure (Art 17): delete when: no longer needed for original purpose, consent withdrawn, unlawful processing. Exceptions: legal retention obligations (financial records), legal claims, public interest. Partial deletion is permitted — retain only what the law requires." }, { q: "Data minimisation benefits include:", opts: ["A. Faster database queries only", "B. Smaller breach scope AND smaller attack surface — privacy and security principle", "C. Lower hardware costs only", "D. Simpler backup procedures"], answer: "B", explain: "Data minimisation: collect only what you need. Privacy: GDPR compliance. Security: breach of a small dataset is less damaging than a large one. Every stored data item is a liability that must be protected, backed up, and eventually destroyed. Don\'t collect what you don\'t need." }, { q: "Cryptographic erasure destroys data by:", opts: ["A. Overwriting with random patterns 7 times", "B. Encrypting all data then destroying the key — data unrecoverable without key", "C. Shredding the physical storage", "D. Running degauss coil over the drive"], answer: "B", explain: "Cryptographic erasure: entire drive encrypted, then key destroyed. Without the key, data is mathematically unrecoverable. Excellent for: cloud storage (can\'t destroy hardware), SSDs (wear leveling makes overwriting unreliable), large-scale disposal." }, { q: "PCI DSS prohibits storing:", opts: ["A. Card numbers with any method", "B. CVV/CVC security codes after transaction authorisation — even encrypted", "C. Expiry dates under any circumstances", "D. Cardholder names in databases"], answer: "B", explain: "PCI DSS Req 3: NEVER store CVV/CVC/CVV2 after authorisation — prohibited regardless of encryption method. Card numbers (PAN) can be stored if encrypted. Expiry dates can be stored. Cardholder names can be stored. But CVV: absolutely never stored." }, { q: "Privacy by design means:", opts: ["A. Making the privacy policy page prominent", "B. Incorporating privacy controls into system design from the start — not added later", "C. Hiring a dedicated privacy team", "D. Designing private networks only"], answer: "B", explain: "Privacy by design (GDPR Art 25, Ann Cavoukian): privacy considerations built into requirements, architecture, and design phases. Data minimisation by default, encryption by default, access controls by default. Far cheaper to build in than to retrofit. Default settings should be most privacy-protective." } ] }, { id: "11-40", week: 11, day: 40, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Endpoint Security — Hardening, EDR & Patch Management", objective: "Master endpoint hardening, EDR capabilities, patch management priority, and application control.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 3.1 Infrastructure Security", notes: `## Endpoint Hardening Checklist\n\n**OS:** Remove unnecessary services, apply CIS Benchmarks, disable default admin accounts, enable host-based firewall, full-disk encryption, Secure Boot, NTP sync.\n\n**Users:** Strong password policy, MFA, no local admin rights, separate admin accounts, account lockout policy.\n\n**Applications:** Uninstall unnecessary software, keep all software updated, disable AutoRun/AutoPlay, block Office macros by default, application allowlisting.\n\n---\n\n## Application Control\n\n**Allowlisting (default-deny):** Only approved apps run. Unknown = blocked. Even zero-day malware is blocked if not listed. Best for servers.\n\n**Blocklisting (default-allow):** Known bad apps blocked. Easier to manage but misses unknowns. Antivirus signature model.\n\n**Sandboxing:** Run untrusted apps in isolated environment. Cannot affect host OS.\n\n---\n\n## EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)\n\nBeyond traditional AV:\n- Behavioural analysis: malicious behaviour patterns, not just signatures\n- Memory analysis: detects fileless malware in RAM\n- Process monitoring: parent-child relationships, injection\n- Network monitoring: C2 communication detection\n- Automated response: isolate endpoint, kill process, remove file\n\n**Traditional AV vs EDR:** AV = signature files only. EDR = behaviour + memory + network + automated response.\n\n**XDR:** EDR expanded across email, network, cloud — unified visibility.\n\n**Fileless malware:** Runs entirely in RAM using LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries — PowerShell, WMI). No file written = AV misses it. EDR detects via process behaviour monitoring.\n\n---\n\n## Patch Management\n\n1. Inventory — know all assets and software versions\n2. Monitor — CVE feeds, vendor advisories\n3. Test — staging before production\n4. Deploy — WSUS, SCCM, Ansible\n5. Verify — confirm successful application\n6. Report — compliance dashboard\n\n**Priority SLAs:**\n- Critical + actively exploited: 24-72 hours\n- High CVSS: 7 days\n- Medium: 30 days\n- Low: next maintenance cycle\n\n---\n\n## Host-Based Controls\n\n**HIDS:** Host intrusion detection — alerts on suspicious activity (file changes, anomalies). Cannot block.\n**HIPS:** Host intrusion prevention — alerts AND blocks automatically. False positive risk.\n**FIM (File Integrity Monitoring):** Alerts when critical system files change. Detects rootkits and persistence.`, exercise: { title: "Endpoint Security Hardening Scenarios", instructions: "Apply the correct endpoint security control.", items: [ "New workstation deployed with defaults. First 5 hardening actions?", "AV shows clean but system is slow with outbound traffic to unknown IP. What is likely happening?", "Company wants to prevent ANY unauthorised software on servers. Which application control?", "CVSS 9.8 vulnerability disclosed Tuesday. Patch cycle is monthly. What should happen?", "Ransomware begins encrypting files. What EDR capability should trigger?", "What is fileless malware and why does traditional AV miss it?", "HIDS vs HIPS — key operational difference?", "Developer has local admin rights on their laptop. Why is this a security risk?" ], answer: `1. (1) Change all default credentials (local admin, BIOS, management interfaces). (2) Apply all OS and software updates. (3) Enable full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault). (4) Enable and configure host-based firewall. (5) Remove unnecessary software and services. 2. Fileless malware. No malicious file exists for AV to detect. Malware runs in memory via PowerShell or legitimate processes. EDR with behavioural analysis detects: unusual PowerShell execution, suspicious process injection, C2 network connections from unexpected processes. 3. Application allowlisting (default-deny). Only explicitly listed applications can execute. Unknown = blocked automatically. Even zero-day malware is blocked because it\'s not on the approved list. More restrictive but far more effective for servers with known, static application sets. 4. Emergency out-of-cycle patch. CVSS 9.8 cannot wait 30 days. SLA: 24-72 hours. Brief test in staging if possible, deploy to critical exposed systems first, then broad rollout. Update patching SLAs to include emergency procedures for critical/actively-exploited CVEs. 5. Automated endpoint isolation. EDR detects ransomware behaviour (rapid file encryption pattern, known process names, abnormal I/O). Automatic response: isolate endpoint from network (while keeping EDR management channel active), kill malicious process, alert SOC. Contains ransomware in seconds, preventing network share encryption. 6. Fileless malware lives in RAM only — no files written to disk. Uses: PowerShell scripts, WMI commands, legitimate system tools (LOLBins). Traditional AV scans files — nothing to scan. EDR detects: unusual PowerShell command flags, Office spawning PowerShell, memory injection into legitimate processes. 7. HIDS: detects and ALERTS — analyst must investigate and respond manually. HIPS: detects AND BLOCKS automatically. HIPS can block legitimate activity if misconfigured (false positive risk). HIDS is safer to start with; tune to HIPS once false positive rate is acceptable. 8. Local admin = if user session is compromised (phishing, web exploit), attacker inherits admin rights. Can: install malware, disable security tools, dump credentials (Mimikatz), pivot laterally. Use standard user account for daily work. Separate admin account used only for explicit admin tasks (principle of least privilege).` }, practical: { title: "Endpoint Hardening Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Audit endpoint security posture", command: `echo "=== ENDPOINT SECURITY AUDIT ===" echo -e "\n1. Listening services (attack surface):" ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep LISTEN | awk '{print " ",$4}' | head -10 echo -e "\n2. Users with sudo access (privileged accounts):" getent group sudo 2>/dev/null || getent group wheel 2>/dev/null echo -e "\n3. SSH security settings:" sudo grep -E "PermitRootLogin|PasswordAuthentication|MaxAuthTries" /etc/ssh/sshd_config 2>/dev/null echo -e "\n4. Firewall status:" sudo ufw status 2>/dev/null | head -5 echo -e "\n5. Available security patches:" apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | grep -i security | wc -l | xargs echo "Security updates available:"`, explain: "This audit covers five key hardening domains: open ports (attack surface reduction), privilege management (who has sudo), SSH security (should have no root login, key auth only), firewall status (should be active with default deny), and patch status (all security updates should be applied)." }, { instruction: "Configure file integrity monitoring", command: `echo "=== FILE INTEGRITY MONITORING CONCEPT ===" echo "Critical files to monitor:" for f in /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/sudoers; do if [ -f "$f" ]; then h=$(sha256sum "$f" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}') echo " $f" echo " Baseline hash: $(echo $h | head -c 32)..." fi done echo "" echo "Changes to these files indicate:" echo " /etc/passwd — new user created (persistence)" echo " /etc/shadow — password modified" echo " /etc/sudoers — new privileged user added" echo "" echo "FIM tools: AIDE, Tripwire, Wazuh FIM module" echo "SIEM integration: FIM alerts → SIEM → SOC investigation"`, explain: "File integrity monitoring creates cryptographic baselines. Any change to /etc/passwd could mean an attacker added a persistence account. Changed /etc/sudoers = new privileged access. Modified system binaries = rootkit. FIM alerts must go to SIEM for immediate investigation." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "EDR advantage over traditional antivirus:", opts: ["A. Uses larger signature databases", "B. Behavioural detection, memory analysis, automated response — catches fileless and zero-day threats", "C. Cheaper licensing", "D. Requires less system resources"], answer: "B", explain: "Traditional AV: file signature matching. Misses zero-days and fileless malware. EDR: monitors process behaviour, memory, network connections. Detects malicious patterns without signatures. Can automatically isolate endpoint when threat detected." }, { q: "Application allowlisting (default-deny) provides:", opts: ["A. Easy management — approve everything by default", "B. Only approved applications execute — unknown malware blocked automatically", "C. Protection against known malware only", "D. Faster application launch times"], answer: "B", explain: "Allowlisting: nothing runs unless explicitly approved. Even novel malware with no signature is blocked — it\'s not on the approved list. More restrictive to manage but far more effective. Ideal for servers where the application set is known and stable." }, { q: "Fileless malware evades traditional AV because:", opts: ["A. It is too small to detect", "B. Runs entirely in memory using legitimate tools — no files for AV to scan", "C. It disables AV on execution", "D. It uses valid digital signatures"], answer: "B", explain: "Fileless: executes via PowerShell, WMI, certutil — built-in Windows tools (LOLBins). No malicious files written to disk. AV scans files — nothing to find. EDR detects: unusual PowerShell command-line arguments, Office applications spawning PowerShell, suspicious process injection." }, { q: "Emergency patch SLA for CVSS 9.8 actively exploited:", opts: ["A. Next monthly cycle", "B. 90 days per standard guidance", "C. 24-72 hours — cannot wait", "D. Only after vendor confirms stability"], answer: "C", explain: "Actively exploited critical CVEs: patch within 24-72 hours. Attackers are exploiting it NOW. Compare risk: exploitation (very high, immediate) vs patch disruption (moderate, manageable). Test briefly in staging but prioritise speed. Update patch SLAs to mandate emergency out-of-cycle patching." }, { q: "File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) detects:", opts: ["A. Network intrusions", "B. Unauthorised changes to critical system files — rootkits, backdoors, new accounts", "C. Password brute-force attempts", "D. Application performance degradation"], answer: "B", explain: "FIM: cryptographic baseline of critical files. Any change = alert. Attackers establishing persistence modify: /etc/passwd (new user), /etc/sudoers (new privilege), system binaries (rootkit). FIM catches these. Alerts must flow to SIEM for immediate investigation." }, { q: "Local admin rights on user workstations should be removed because:", opts: ["A. Standard users are more productive without admin rights", "B. Compromised session inherits admin rights — malware has full OS control, can disable security tools", "C. Admins need remote access to all machines", "D. Admin rights slow down workstations"], answer: "B", explain: "If a user with local admin is phished and clicks malware, the malware runs with admin privileges: installs rootkits, disables AV, dumps credentials (Mimikatz), spreads laterally. Standard user + separate admin account = blast radius dramatically reduced." }, { q: "HIPS differs from HIDS by:", opts: ["A. HIPS only monitors network traffic", "B. HIPS blocks malicious activity automatically; HIDS only alerts", "C. HIDS is more accurate", "D. HIPS only works on servers"], answer: "B", explain: "HIDS: detects suspicious activity, generates alert, waits for analyst. HIPS: detects AND automatically blocks. HIPS more effective but misconfiguration can block legitimate activity (false positives). Start with HIDS, tune rules, then move to HIPS block mode." }, { q: "AutoRun/AutoPlay should be disabled to prevent:", opts: ["A. Network-based attacks", "B. Malware on removable media auto-executing on insertion", "C. Browser-based exploits", "D. Phishing attacks"], answer: "B", explain: "AutoRun: Windows automatically executes programs from removable media on insertion. Used by USB worms (Conficker) and baiting attacks. Disable via Group Policy: malicious USB plugged in won\'t auto-execute. User must manually navigate to and execute malware." }, { q: "CIS Benchmarks provide:", opts: ["A. CVE severity scores", "B. Prescriptive security configuration standards for OS and applications", "C. Network performance metrics", "D. Regulatory compliance frameworks"], answer: "B", explain: "CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks: detailed, consensus-based hardening guidance for specific OS versions (Windows 11, Ubuntu 22.04), applications (Apache, SQL Server), and cloud platforms. Used to audit systems against a known secure baseline and measure hardening progress." }, { q: "Patch management step after verification is:", opts: ["A. Deploy to production", "B. Test in staging", "C. Report — track compliance percentage and document in patch management system", "D. Notify users of the patch"], answer: "C", explain: "Patch management lifecycle: Inventory → Monitor → Test (staging) → Deploy → VERIFY (confirm applied) → REPORT (track compliance percentage, document for audits). Reporting proves compliance to auditors and identifies systems still needing patches." } ] }, { id: "11-41", week: 11, day: 41, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Resilience, Backup Strategy & Business Continuity", objective: "Understand redundancy designs, backup types, the 3-2-1 rule, disaster recovery planning, and DR testing.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 3.5 Resilience and Recovery", notes: `## Redundancy Types\n\n**RAID:**\n- RAID 0: Striping — performance, NO redundancy\n- RAID 1: Mirroring — exact copy, can lose all but one drive\n- RAID 5: Striping + parity — can lose 1 drive (minimum 3 drives)\n- RAID 6: Double parity — can lose 2 drives (minimum 4 drives)\n- RAID 10: Mirror + stripe — can lose 1 from each mirrored pair\n\n**Power:** Redundant PSUs (N+1), UPS, generator.\n**Network:** Dual ISPs, LACP link aggregation, redundant switches.\n**Geographic:** Active-Active (both sites serving), Active-Passive (primary + standby).\n\n---\n\n## Backup Strategy\n\n**Types:**\n- Full: Complete copy. Fast restore, large storage, slow backup.\n- Incremental: Changes since LAST backup. Fast backup, slow restore (need full + all incrementals).\n- Differential: Changes since last FULL. Faster restore than incremental, larger than incremental.\n\n**3-2-1 Rule:** 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 offsite.\n\n**Immutable backups:** Cannot be modified/deleted for set period. Ransomware-resistant even with admin access.\n\n**Testing:** Backups must be restored and tested regularly. Untested backups frequently fail.\n\n---\n\n## DR Planning\n\n**DR site types:**\n- Hot: Fully operational, real-time sync. Minutes to failover. Highest cost.\n- Warm: Equipment ready, recent data. Hours to failover. Medium cost.\n- Cold: Empty facility. Days to provision. Lowest cost.\n\n**DR testing types:**\n- Tabletop exercise: Discussion-based. No systems involved. Finds procedure gaps.\n- Walkthrough: More hands-on procedure review.\n- Parallel test: DR systems activated alongside production — verify they work without disrupting production.\n- Full interruption: Production shut down, recover from DR only. Highest realism, highest risk.\n\n**Key metrics:**\n- MTD: Maximum Tolerable Downtime — longest acceptable outage\n- RTO: Must be ≤ MTD\n- RPO: Maximum data loss acceptable → determines backup frequency`, exercise: { title: "Resilience and DR Design", instructions: "Apply the correct resilience or DR concept.", items: [ "RAID 0 array for all company data. What is the availability risk?", "Company has backups but never tests restoration. Ransomware hits. What problem?", "Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule — why each component.", "Ransomware admin access encrypts all backup files on same server. What prevents this?", "Tabletop vs full interruption DR test — when to choose each?", "RAID 5 with 4 drives — how many can fail before data loss?", "RTO=4 hours but DR plan uses cold site. Achievable?", "What is multi-cloud redundancy and what risk does it address?" ], answer: `1. Critical risk: RAID 0 has ZERO redundancy. Any single drive failure destroys ALL data. RAID 0 only provides performance (striping). Change to: RAID 1 (simple mirror), RAID 5 (balanced), RAID 10 (high-performance + redundancy). Implement proper offsite backups regardless of RAID level. 2. Backup restoration failure. Untested backups fail for many reasons: corrupt media, incomplete backup jobs never monitored, wrong scope (missed critical database), expired cloud credentials, software incompatibility after OS upgrade. "We have backups" ≠ "We can restore." 3. 3-2-1: (3) Three copies — single backup failure destroys your only copy. (2) Two media types — ransomware encrypts disk but not offline tape; fire destroys on-premise but not cloud. (1) One offsite — site-level disaster (fire, flood) doesn\'t destroy all copies. Last line of defence. 4. Immutable backups (WORM storage). Cannot be modified or deleted for a retention period even by admin. Ransomware with admin rights can encrypt standard backups. Air-gapped backups (physically disconnected) also work. Modern cloud backup services offer immutability features (Object Lock, Vault Lock). 5. Tabletop: regular practice (quarterly/annually), finds gaps in procedures, trains staff, zero production risk. Full interruption: real proof DR works — do annually, avoid peak periods, never do first without tabletop prep first. Full interruption is high risk (actual production shutdown). 6. RAID 5 can lose 1 drive. RAID 5 distributes parity across all drives. One drive fails = rebuild from parity. Second failure before rebuild = data loss. RAID 6 = double parity = can lose 2 drives. 7. NO — cold site cannot support 4-hour RTO. Cold site = empty facility, days to provision hardware and restore data. For 4-hour RTO: need warm site (hours) or hot site (minutes). DRP must align RTO with DR site capability. 8. Multi-cloud: distribute workloads across AWS + Azure + GCP. Mitigates: cloud provider outage (if AWS region fails, Azure continues). Also mitigates provider-specific vulnerabilities, lock-in, and pricing. Significantly more complex to operate and secure.` }, practical: { title: "Backup and RAID Concepts Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Implement and verify a backup with integrity check", command: `mkdir -p /tmp/src /tmp/bak echo "Critical production data" > /tmp/src/data.db echo "Application config" > /tmp/src/config.conf echo -e "\n=== FULL BACKUP WITH HASH ===" tar -czf /tmp/bak/full.tar.gz -C /tmp src sha256sum /tmp/bak/full.tar.gz > /tmp/bak/full.sha256 echo "Backup created and hashed" echo -e "\n=== VERIFY INTEGRITY ===" sha256sum -c /tmp/bak/full.sha256 && echo "PASS" || echo "FAIL - backup corrupted" echo -e "\n=== TEST RESTORATION ===" tar -xzf /tmp/bak/full.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore_test 2>/dev/null || mkdir -p /tmp/restore_test && tar -xzf /tmp/bak/full.tar.gz -C /tmp ls /tmp/src/ | while read f; do cmp /tmp/src/$f /tmp/restore_test/src/$f 2>/dev/null && echo "$f: RESTORED OK" || echo "$f: RESTORE FAILED"; done`, explain: "Complete backup lifecycle: create, hash, verify integrity, and TEST RESTORATION. The sha256sum check detects corruption. The restoration test confirms you can actually recover — this is what most organisations skip. Untested backups fail when you need them most." }, { instruction: "RAID trade-off calculator", command: `python3 << 'EOF' configs = [ (0, 4, 1000, 0, "NO redundancy — any failure = data loss"), (1, 2, 1000, 1, "Full mirror — 50% overhead"), (5, 4, 1000, 1, "1 drive parity — can lose 1"), (6, 4, 1000, 2, "2 drive parity — can lose 2"), (10,4, 1000, 1, "Mirror+stripe — lose 1 per mirrored pair"), ] print(f"{'RAID':6} {'Drives':7} {'Usable GB':12} {'Max Fail':10} Notes") print("-" * 65) for raid, drives, size, can_fail, note in configs: if raid == 0: usable = drives * size elif raid == 1: usable = size elif raid == 5: usable = (drives-1)*size elif raid == 6: usable = (drives-2)*size elif raid == 10:usable = (drives//2)*size print(f"RAID {raid:<2} {drives:>5} {usable:>8} {can_fail:>4} {note}") EOF`, explain: "RAID trade-offs: RAID 0 gives max capacity/speed but zero fault tolerance. RAID 5 is the enterprise sweet spot — good capacity, decent performance, 1-drive tolerance. RAID 6 for critical data needing 2-drive tolerance. RAID 10 for databases needing both performance and redundancy." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "RAID 5 minimum drives and fault tolerance:", opts: ["A. 2 minimum, can lose 1", "B. 3 minimum, can lose 1", "C. 4 minimum, can lose 2", "D. 3 minimum, can lose 2"], answer: "B", explain: "RAID 5: minimum 3 drives. Parity distributed across all drives. Capacity = (n-1) × drive size. Can tolerate 1 drive failure — rebuild from parity. 2nd failure before rebuild = data loss. RAID 6 = 4 drives minimum, tolerates 2 failures." }, { q: "3-2-1 backup rule means:", opts: ["A. 3 daily, 2 weekly, 1 monthly backup", "B. 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 copy offsite", "C. 3 backup servers, 2 sites, 1 cloud copy", "D. 3-week retention, 2-day RPO, 1-hour RTO"], answer: "B", explain: "3-2-1: Three copies (original + 2 backups), two media types (disk + cloud, disk + tape), one offsite. Three copies: single backup failure doesn\'t leave you with zero. Two media: ransomware/fire won\'t destroy all copies. One offsite: site disaster covered." }, { q: "Immutable backups resist ransomware because:", opts: ["A. They are stored on separate network", "B. Cannot be modified or deleted for retention period — even admin cannot encrypt or delete them", "C. They use stronger encryption", "D. They are stored offline always"], answer: "B", explain: "WORM (Write Once Read Many) storage: data can be written once, never modified or deleted for the retention period. Even a ransomware actor with full admin access cannot encrypt or delete immutable backups. Separate from air-gapped backups which are physically disconnected." }, { q: "Tabletop DR exercise vs full interruption test:", opts: ["A. Tabletop requires production systems offline", "B. Tabletop = discussion-based, no systems involved; full interruption = production shut down, recover from DR", "C. They are the same", "D. Full interruption is safer than tabletop"], answer: "B", explain: "Tabletop: discussion-based walkthrough, finds procedure gaps, zero risk, can do quarterly. Full interruption: shut down production, prove DR works end-to-end, highest realism, significant risk (actual production unavailability). Never do full interruption without tabletop preparation first." }, { q: "RAID 0 is inappropriate for production data because:", opts: ["A. Too slow for production workloads", "B. No redundancy — any single drive failure destroys all data on the array", "C. Requires too many drives", "D. Incompatible with enterprise storage arrays"], answer: "B", explain: "RAID 0: striping for performance, zero fault tolerance. If any ONE drive fails, the entire array\'s data is gone permanently. Use only for: scratch space, temp storage, or as part of RAID 10. NEVER as the only storage for important data." }, { q: "MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime) vs RTO relationship:", opts: ["A. RTO must always exceed MTD", "B. RTO must be ≤ MTD — recovery must complete before tolerable downtime expires", "C. They are unrelated metrics", "D. MTD is always set to twice the RTO"], answer: "B", explain: "MTD: maximum acceptable outage before catastrophic business impact. RTO: target recovery time. RTO must be ≤ MTD. If MTD=4 hours and RTO=8 hours, you\'ll exceed tolerable downtime before recovery completes. DRP must align site type with RTO requirement." }, { q: "Full backup vs differential backup restore speed:", opts: ["A. Differential is always slower", "B. Full backup restores from one set; differential needs full + one differential (faster than incremental)", "C. They restore equally fast", "D. Incremental is faster than differential to restore"], answer: "B", explain: "Full: restore from single set — fastest restore. Incremental: need full + EVERY incremental since full — slowest restore. Differential: need full + MOST RECENT differential — faster than incremental. Trade-off: storage space vs restore time." }, { q: "Parallel DR test is preferred over full interruption test because:", opts: ["A. It is more realistic than full interruption", "B. Production continues while DR systems are validated — lower risk with good realism", "C. It requires fewer resources", "D. It can be done without management approval"], answer: "B", explain: "Parallel test: activate DR systems alongside production — verify they can handle the workload without affecting actual production. Good realism. Full interruption: production stops, all traffic switches to DR — maximum realism, maximum risk. Use parallel before progressing to full interruption." }, { q: "Multi-cloud redundancy primarily addresses:", opts: ["A. Application security vulnerabilities", "B. Cloud provider outages — workloads continue on other providers if one fails", "C. Data sovereignty requirements", "D. Cost optimization"], answer: "B", explain: "Multi-cloud: workloads across AWS + Azure + GCP. If one provider has an outage (AWS us-east-1 has had major outages), workloads continue on others. Eliminates cloud provider as single point of failure. More complex and expensive to operate." }, { q: "Untested backups frequently fail because:", opts: ["A. Backup media degrades quickly", "B. Corruption, incomplete jobs, credential expiry, software incompatibilities are undetected without testing", "C. Backup software has poor reliability", "D. Network interruptions corrupt backup data"], answer: "B", explain: "Untested backup failure modes: silent corruption, incomplete backup jobs not monitored, cloud credential expiration, software version incompatibilities after OS upgrade, wrong backup scope (critical database excluded). Test restoration quarterly minimum. The only backup that matters is one you\'ve proven you can restore from." } ] }, { id: "10-36", week: 10, day: 36, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Wireless, Mobile & Embedded Security", objective: "Understand mobile device management, BYOD security, IoT/embedded system threats, and secure wireless enterprise deployment.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 3.4 Mobile and Embedded Security", notes: `## Mobile Device Management (MDM)\n\n**MDM:** Software managing mobile devices across an organisation. Capabilities:\n- Enforce encryption on device storage\n- Push security policies (screen lock, complex passwords)\n- Remote wipe (full wipe or selective/container wipe)\n- App allowlisting/blocklisting\n- Geo-fencing (disable device outside approved areas)\n- Certificate deployment\n\n**MAM (Mobile Application Management):** Manage only the applications, not the full device. Useful for BYOD.\n\n**UEM (Unified Endpoint Management):** Manages ALL endpoints: phones, tablets, laptops, desktops, IoT from one console.\n\n---\n\n## BYOD, COPE, CYOD Models\n\n**BYOD (Bring Your Own Device):** Employee uses personal device for work.\n- Lowest cost for organisation\n- Privacy concerns — MDM can wipe personal data\n- Hardest to secure\n\n**COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled):** Company provides device, allows personal use.\n- Good balance: corporate control, employee flexibility\n\n**CYOD (Choose Your Own Device):** Employee chooses from approved list, company owns.\n- Better security than BYOD\n\n**Company-owned, company-use only:** Strictest control. Best security.\n\n---\n\n## Mobile Security Threats\n\n**Jailbreaking (iOS) / Rooting (Android):** Removes OS security controls. Bypasses app sandboxing. MDM may detect and block.\n\n**Side-loading:** Installing apps from outside official app store. Bypasses vetting. Source of malware.\n\n**Evil twin Wi-Fi:** Mobile devices auto-connect to known SSIDs. Attacker creates network with same name.\n\n**SMS phishing (smishing):** Malicious links via text message.\n\n**Rogue app:** Legitimate-looking app with malicious code. In third-party app stores or via side-loading.\n\n---\n\n## IoT Security Challenges\n\n**Problem areas:**\n- Default credentials (admin/admin, admin/password) — never changed\n- No patch mechanism — firmware cannot be updated\n- Weak or no encryption on communications\n- Long lifecycle — deployed for 10-20 years\n- Constrained resources — no room for security agents\n\n**Attack vectors:** Default credentials → remote access. Unencrypted traffic → sniffing. Known CVEs with no patches available.\n\n**Mitigations:**\n1. Change default credentials immediately\n2. Network segmentation — IoT on separate VLAN\n3. Firewall rules restricting IoT to minimum required ports\n4. Disable unused features (Telnet, UPnP, web admin)\n5. Monitor for unusual traffic from IoT devices\n\n---\n\n## Embedded System Security\n\n**SCADA/ICS (Industrial Control Systems):** Control physical processes — power plants, water treatment, manufacturing. Historically air-gapped, now increasingly networked. Stuxnet proved they can be compromised.\n\n**RTOS (Real-Time Operating System):** Deterministic timing for critical processes. Limited security features.\n\n**HSM (Hardware Security Module):** Dedicated hardware for cryptographic operations. Stores keys in tamper-proof hardware. Never extracts private keys.\n\n**TPM (Trusted Platform Module):** Security chip on motherboard. Stores cryptographic keys, measures boot integrity. Used for BitLocker, Secure Boot.`, exercise: { title: "Mobile and IoT Security Scenarios", instructions: "Identify the correct control, attack, or recommendation for each scenario.", items: [ "An employee's BYOD phone is lost with company email configured. The phone has no screen lock. What MDM capability is needed immediately?", "A hospital has 500 IoT medical devices with default credentials running on the same network as patient records. What is the priority risk and mitigation?", "A user jailbreaks their iPhone to install apps outside the App Store. What security controls has this circumvented?", "A factory's SCADA system was previously air-gapped but is now connected to the corporate network for remote monitoring. What new risk was introduced?", "MDM vs MAM for a law firm's BYOD policy — which is more privacy-friendly for employees?", "What is an HSM and why is it preferable to storing private keys in software?", "A mobile app stores an AWS access key hardcoded in the app binary. What vulnerability and why?", "Secure Boot uses the TPM to do what specific security function?" ], answer: `1. Remote wipe. MDM can issue a command to wipe the device remotely even if the screen is unlocked. Selective wipe removes only corporate data and apps while preserving personal data. Full wipe restores factory settings. This is a key reason corporate MDM must be installed before allowing access to corporate email. 2. Priority risk: an attacker compromising an IoT device (via default credentials) can use it as a pivot point to attack patient record systems on the same network. The IoT devices are on the same flat network as sensitive data. Mitigation: (1) Change ALL default credentials immediately. (2) Segment IoT devices onto a dedicated VLAN with firewall rules blocking access to patient records. This is the single highest-impact mitigation. 3. Jailbreaking circumvents: (1) App store vetting — can install unsigned, unreviewed apps. (2) App sandboxing — apps can access other apps' data. (3) Code signing requirements. (4) MDM detection and enforcement (some MDMs detect jailbreak). (5) OS-level security updates compatibility. This is why MDM can be configured to deny access to corporate resources on jailbroken devices. 4. The air gap was the primary security control. Connecting SCADA to corporate network introduces: (1) The entire internet attack surface via the corporate network. (2) Ability for malware to spread from corporate to SCADA. (3) Remote exploitation of SCADA vulnerabilities (previously theoretical). Stuxnet targeted exactly this scenario. Mitigation: data diode (one-way), industrial DMZ, strict whitelisting. 5. MAM (Mobile Application Management). MDM manages the entire device — can wipe ALL data including personal photos/messages. Employees rightfully object to this on personal devices. MAM creates a secure container for corporate apps and data. The container can be wiped remotely without touching personal data. Better employee acceptance for BYOD. 6. HSM = Hardware Security Module. Dedicated tamper-proof hardware designed specifically for cryptographic operations. Private keys are generated inside the HSM and NEVER exported — all crypto operations happen inside the hardware. Even with physical access, keys cannot be extracted. Software key storage: keys are files on disk, accessible to OS, vulnerable to malware, memory dumps. HSM is orders of magnitude more secure. 7. Hardcoded credentials in mobile app binary = major vulnerability. The app binary can be decompiled with trivial tools (apktool, jadx). Anyone who downloads the app can extract the AWS access key. With that key, they have AWS access. Apps are distributed to millions of users = millions of attackers potentially. Fix: never hardcode credentials, use server-side token vending, use AWS Cognito or similar for mobile authentication. 8. Secure Boot uses TPM to: (1) Store cryptographic measurements of the bootloader and OS kernel. (2) During boot, measure each component and compare to stored values. (3) If measurements don't match (boot image tampered), Secure Boot halts. Prevents: bootkits, rootkits that modify the bootloader, and offline attacks on the OS. The TPM is the hardware root of trust.` }, practical: { title: "Mobile and IoT Security Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Scan for IoT devices with default credentials (on your own network)", command: `sudo apt install nmap -y 2>/dev/null echo "=== IoT Network Discovery ===" # Discover devices on local subnet (your network only) LOCAL_NET=$(ip route show | grep "proto kernel" | head -1 | awk '{print $1}') echo "Scanning: $LOCAL_NET" # Quick discovery scan sudo nmap -sn "$LOCAL_NET" 2>/dev/null | \ grep -E "Nmap scan|Host is up|MAC Address" | head -20 echo -e "\n=== Common IoT Default Credential Ports ===" echo "Port 23 (Telnet) - most dangerous: cleartext admin" echo "Port 80/443 (Web UI) - check for default admin/password" echo "Port 22 (SSH) - check for default credentials" echo "Port 8080/8443 (Alt HTTP) - router admin panels" echo "Port 554 (RTSP) - IP cameras" echo "" echo "IoT best practice: every device on dedicated VLAN" echo "Firewall rule: IoT VLAN cannot reach corporate network"`, explain: "IoT devices with default credentials are one of the most common enterprise security failures. Cameras, printers, smart TVs — all with admin/admin or admin/password. Once compromised, they provide network access inside your perimeter. Network segmentation limits the blast radius." }, { instruction: "Demonstrate mobile app security concept — certificate pinning", command: `python3 << 'EOF' import ssl, socket, hashlib def get_cert_fingerprint(hostname, port=443): """Get SHA-256 fingerprint of server's TLS certificate""" try: context = ssl.create_default_context() with socket.create_connection((hostname, port), timeout=5) as sock: with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=hostname) as ssock: cert_der = ssock.getpeercert(binary_form=True) fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(cert_der).hexdigest() return fingerprint except Exception as e: return f"Error: {e}" # Simulate certificate pinning PINNED_CERT = {} # In production: hardcoded during app build print("=== Certificate Pinning Concept ===\n") hosts = ["google.com", "github.com"] for host in hosts: fp = get_cert_fingerprint(host) print(f"Certificate fingerprint for {host}:") print(f" {fp}") if host not in PINNED_CERT: PINNED_CERT[host] = fp print(f" [First run] Pinned this certificate") elif PINNED_CERT[host] == fp: print(f" [Subsequent run] Certificate matches pin - TRUSTED") else: print(f" [ATTACK DETECTED] Certificate changed - BLOCKING!") print("\nCertificate pinning: even a valid CA-signed cert fails if it doesn't match the pin") print("This blocks MITM attacks using rogue certificates from compromised CAs") EOF`, explain: "Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected certificate fingerprint in the app. The first time connecting to google.com, we pin its fingerprint. On future connections, if the certificate changes (MITM attack with rogue cert, even from a trusted CA), the mismatch is detected and the connection is blocked." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "MDM remote wipe capability is critical for BYOD because:", opts: ["A. It speeds up the device", "B. It allows organisations to remove corporate data from lost/stolen devices", "C. It prevents jailbreaking", "D. It encrypts all personal data"], answer: "B", explain: "Remote wipe: MDM can erase corporate data from a lost/stolen device. Selective wipe removes only the corporate container. Full wipe restores factory settings. Without this, lost devices with corporate email access are a data breach." }, { q: "The most immediate IoT security action is:", opts: ["A. Install security software on each device", "B. Change all default credentials immediately", "C. Disconnect all IoT devices from the network", "D. Upgrade all IoT firmware"], answer: "B", explain: "Default credentials are IoT's biggest vulnerability. admin/admin or admin/password on network-connected devices gives any attacker on your network (or internet if exposed) full access. Change EVERY default credential before deployment. Priority: immediate, required, non-negotiable." }, { q: "Jailbreaking an iOS device risks:", opts: ["A. Voiding the warranty only", "B. Removing OS security controls including app sandboxing and code signing", "C. Slowing down the device only", "D. Disabling mobile data"], answer: "B", explain: "Jailbreaking: removes Apple's security controls. Consequences: (1) Can install unsigned apps from any source. (2) Apps can escape sandboxes and access other apps' data. (3) MDM security policies may not function. (4) OS updates may break the jailbreak, leaving device unpatched." }, { q: "IoT devices should be placed in a dedicated VLAN because:", opts: ["A. IoT devices use different network protocols", "B. Network segmentation limits blast radius — compromised IoT cannot directly attack other network segments", "C. IoT devices need more bandwidth", "D. To improve IoT performance"], answer: "B", explain: "IoT segmentation: dedicated VLAN with firewall rules. Compromised IoT device stays in the IoT VLAN. Cannot pivot to attack corporate servers or patient records. This containment strategy is the most impactful IoT security control after changing default credentials." }, { q: "COPE mobile device model means:", opts: ["A. Customer-Owned, Personal Encrypted", "B. Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled — company provides device, allows personal use", "C. Company-Only, Personal Excluded", "D. Customer-Oriented Portable Equipment"], answer: "B", explain: "COPE: organisation owns and controls the device (can enforce all security policies, full MDM management) but allows personal use. Good balance between security and employee satisfaction. More secure than BYOD, more flexible than company-only." }, { q: "An HSM (Hardware Security Module) provides what advantage over software key storage?", opts: ["A. HSMs are faster at encryption", "B. Private keys never leave the hardware — operations happen inside tamper-proof module, keys cannot be extracted", "C. HSMs are cheaper", "D. HSMs work without electricity"], answer: "B", explain: "HSM: tamper-proof hardware. Keys are generated and stored inside — NEVER exported. All crypto operations (sign, decrypt) happen inside the HSM. Even with physical access, keys cannot be extracted. Software keys: stored as files, accessible to OS, vulnerable to malware and memory dumps." }, { q: "TPM (Trusted Platform Module) enables Secure Boot by:", opts: ["A. Encrypting the hard drive automatically", "B. Measuring and storing boot component hashes — detects tampering if values change", "C. Requiring a PIN at every boot", "D. Blocking network access until fully booted"], answer: "B", explain: "Secure Boot: TPM measures (hashes) each component during boot (bootloader, OS kernel). These measurements are compared to stored expected values. If any component was tampered with, measurements don't match — boot is halted. Prevents bootkits and rootkits that survive OS reinstalls." }, { q: "BYOD compared to COPE provides the organisation with:", opts: ["A. More security control", "B. Less security control but lower device cost", "C. Better compliance with regulations", "D. Simpler MDM management"], answer: "B", explain: "BYOD: employee's personal device. Organisation has limited control — cannot enforce full MDM policies, employee may object to monitoring, personal/corporate data mixed. Lower cost (no device purchase). COPE: full control but organisation pays for device." }, { q: "SCADA/ICS systems are high-value targets because:", opts: ["A. They contain valuable financial data", "B. Compromising them can cause physical damage to critical infrastructure", "C. They are easier to attack than enterprise IT", "D. They are always internet-connected"], answer: "B", explain: "SCADA/ICS control physical processes: power grids, water treatment, pipelines, manufacturing. A cyberattack can cause: physical equipment damage, environmental release of hazardous materials, power outages, or compromise of critical national infrastructure. Stuxnet physically destroyed centrifuges." }, { q: "Side-loading apps on a mobile device means:", opts: ["A. Loading apps while connected to a computer", "B. Installing apps from outside the official app store — bypassing security vetting", "C. Installing the same app on multiple devices simultaneously", "D. Updating apps in the background"], answer: "B", explain: "Side-loading: install APK (Android) or IPA (iOS) directly without going through the official store. Bypasses: malware scanning, privacy review, code signing verification. Source of mobile malware. Enterprise MDM can detect and block side-loaded apps." } ] }, , { id: "11-42", week: 11, day: 42, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Advanced Attacks — DNS, MITM, Credential & Supply Chain", objective: "Master DNS poisoning, SSL stripping, pass-the-hash, Kerberoasting, and supply chain attacks with their mitigations.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — 2.4 Network Attacks", notes: `## DNS Attacks\n\n**DNS poisoning:** Inject false records into resolver cache. All clients redirected to attacker IP. Mitigation: DNSSEC.\n\n**DNS hijacking:** Modify DNS settings on router/ISP/endpoint — all queries go to malicious resolver.\n\n**DNS tunnelling:** Exfiltrate data encoded in DNS queries (data.attacker.com subdomains). Bypasses most firewalls. Detect via DNS query volume monitoring.\n\n---\n\n## ARP Attacks (Layer 2)\n\n**ARP spoofing:** Gratuitous ARP reply maps attacker MAC to victim IP. Intercepts traffic.\nMitigation: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), 802.1X.\n\n**ARP MITM:** Poison both victim and gateway ARP caches. All traffic flows through attacker. Attacker forwards (MITM) or drops (DoS).\n\n---\n\n## MITM Variants\n\n**SSL stripping:** Downgrade HTTPS to HTTP. User's credentials sent cleartext to attacker.\nMitigation: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) — browser refuses HTTP, always forces HTTPS.\n\n**TLS downgrade:** Force weak TLS (1.0, SSL 3.0). Enables POODLE, BEAST attacks.\nMitigation: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1/SSL 3.0. Enforce TLS 1.2+, prefer TLS 1.3.\n\n**Session hijacking:** Steal session cookie, impersonate authenticated user.\nMitigation: Secure+HttpOnly cookie flags, short session timeouts, token rotation.\n\n---\n\n## Windows Credential Attacks\n\n**Pass-the-Hash (PtH):** Capture NTLM hash from memory (Mimikatz). Authenticate directly with hash without cracking password.\nMitigation: Windows Credential Guard, Kerberos over NTLM, restrict local admin reuse across machines.\n\n**Pass-the-Ticket (PtT):** Steal Kerberos TGT from memory. Use ticket to authenticate as that user without the password.\nMitigation: Short ticket lifetimes, Credential Guard, detect unusual ticket usage.\n\n**Kerberoasting:** Request service tickets encrypted with service account password hash. Crack offline.\nMitigation: Service account passwords 25+ random chars, Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).\n\n**Golden Ticket:** Compromise KRBTGT hash. Forge ANY Kerberos ticket for ANY user. Full domain compromise.\nMitigation: Reset KRBTGT hash twice, privileged access workstations, Kerberos Armoring.\n\n---\n\n## Supply Chain Attacks\n\n**SolarWinds (2020):** Backdoor injected into SolarWinds Orion update — 18,000+ organisations compromised via a trusted software update.\n\n**XZ Utils (2024):** Backdoor inserted into widely used Linux compression library by a trusted contributor.\n\n**Mitigations:** Verify software hashes, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), signed updates, vendor security assessments, zero trust for third-party integrations.\n\n---\n\n## Replay Attacks\n\n**Replay:** Capture valid authentication data (token, hash, session ID) and retransmit later to authenticate.\nMitigation: Nonces (number used once), timestamps, short-lived tokens.`, exercise: { title: "Advanced Attack Identification", instructions: "Identify the attack and mitigation for each scenario.", items: [ "A user types the correct bank URL but lands on a phishing page. DNS records are correct on authoritative servers but wrong in the ISP resolver. What attack?", "EDR shows unusual DNS queries to subdomains like aGVsbG8=.attacker.com every 30 seconds. What attack?", "An attacker on the same network intercepts a user\'s HTTP login form — HTTPS was available but not used. Which MITM attack and mitigation?", "A Windows domain service account has password \'ServicePass1\'. An attacker runs Rubeus to extract service tickets. What attack?", "An admin captures the KRBTGT hash from the DC. What ticket can now be forged and what is the impact?", "SolarWinds Orion compromise — what made this attack particularly devastating?", "Pass-the-Hash vs Pass-the-Ticket — what is the key difference?", "An attacker intercepts a session cookie over unsecured Wi-Fi. What cookie attributes would have prevented use of the stolen cookie?" ], answer: `1. DNS cache poisoning. The attacker injected a false A record for the bank domain into the ISP\'s resolver cache. All clients using that resolver are sent to the attacker\'s IP. The authoritative server is correct — only the cached resolver is poisoned. Mitigation: DNSSEC (signs DNS records cryptographically) and short TTLs. 2. DNS tunnelling. Base64-encoded data in subdomains — aGVsbG8= decodes to "hello". The attacker is exfiltrating data (or receiving C2 commands) via DNS queries which pass through most firewalls. Mitigation: DNS monitoring for anomalous query volumes/patterns, DNS filtering (block queries to known malicious resolvers), detect unusually long subdomains. 3. SSL stripping. The site had HTTPS available but the user accessed HTTP, which the attacker intercepted. The attacker forwarded HTTPS to the server while relaying HTTP to the user — capturing credentials in cleartext. Mitigation: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) header — browser remembers to always use HTTPS for this domain and refuses HTTP connections. 4. Kerberoasting. The attacker requested a Kerberos service ticket for the service account — this ticket is encrypted with the service account\'s NTLM hash. With a weak password (\'ServicePass1\'), the ticket can be cracked offline with hashcat in seconds. Mitigation: service account passwords must be 25+ random characters (making cracking infeasible), or use gMSA (Group Managed Service Accounts) with auto-rotated passwords. 5. Golden Ticket. With the KRBTGT hash, the attacker can forge Kerberos TGTs (Ticket Granting Tickets) for ANY user including Domain Admin. These forged tickets are cryptographically valid. Impact: complete domain compromise — can access any resource, as any user, indefinitely. Mitigation: reset KRBTGT account password TWICE (both current and previous hash), monitor for tickets with unusual lifetimes or attributes. 6. Supply chain trust. SolarWinds Orion was trusted security/monitoring software used by government agencies and Fortune 500 companies. The compromised update was digitally signed by SolarWinds — all security controls trusted it. Organisations installed the malicious update as part of normal operations with no suspicion. The attacker (Russian SVR) had 9+ months of undetected access. Trust in the supplier was weaponised. 7. Pass-the-Hash uses the NTLM password hash directly as authentication proof. No need to crack the password. Pass-the-Ticket uses a stolen Kerberos ticket (TGT or service ticket). Both allow authentication as another user without knowing the actual password. PtH only works against NTLM authentication. PtT works against Kerberos-protected resources. 8. The HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie — stops XSS-based cookie theft. The Secure flag ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS — the cookie would not have been transmitted over the unencrypted Wi-Fi. Mitigation: both Secure AND HttpOnly flags on session cookies, plus short session timeouts and session token rotation after authentication.` }, practical: { title: "Network Attack Detection Lab", platform: "Linux terminal", steps: [ { instruction: "Detect ARP spoofing indicators", command: `echo "=== ARP TABLE INSPECTION ===" # View current ARP cache arp -n 2>/dev/null || ip neigh show echo -e "\n=== ARP SPOOFING DETECTION ===" # Check for duplicate MACs (key ARP poisoning indicator) python3 << \'PYEOF\' import subprocess, re from collections import Counter result = subprocess.run([\'ip\', \'neigh\', \'show\'], capture_output=True, text=True) lines = result.stdout.strip().split(\'\n\') macs = {} for line in lines: parts = line.split() if len(parts) >= 5 and parts[4] != \'FAILED\': ip = parts[0] mac = parts[4] if len(parts) > 4 else \'unknown\' if mac != \'FAILED\' and mac != \'lladdr\': if mac in macs: print(f"ALERT: MAC {mac} claimed by multiple IPs: {macs[mac]} AND {ip}") print("This indicates ARP spoofing!") else: macs[mac] = ip print(f"OK: {ip} -> {mac}") \'PYEOF\'`, explain: "ARP spoofing detection: two different IPs with the same MAC address means a device is claiming to be multiple hosts. If the gateway IP and another IP share a MAC, an attacker likely has a MITM position. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches automatically blocks unauthorised ARP replies." }, { instruction: "Check DNS security and detect tunnelling indicators", command: `echo "=== DNS SECURITY RECORDS ===" dig +short TXT _dmarc.google.com 2>/dev/null dig +short TXT google.com 2>/dev/null | grep "v=spf1" echo -e "\n=== DNSSEC VALIDATION ===" dig +dnssec google.com A 2>/dev/null | grep -E "RRSIG|DNSKEY|ad" | head -5 dig @8.8.8.8 +dnssec google.com 2>/dev/null | grep "flags:" | head -3 echo -e "\n=== DNS TUNNELLING INDICATORS ===" echo "Signs of DNS tunnelling:" echo "1. Unusually long subdomain queries (> 50 chars)" echo "2. High entropy subdomains (base64 patterns)" echo "3. High DNS query volume from one host" echo "4. Queries for non-existent TLDs" echo "5. TXT record queries from endpoints" echo "" echo "Detection: monitor with DNS monitoring tools (Zeek, Suricata DNS rules)"`, explain: "DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses. The 'ad' flag in a dig response means DNSSEC validation passed. Without DNSSEC, DNS responses can be poisoned. DNS tunnelling generates distinctive patterns: high-entropy subdomains, unusual query volume, long query strings — all detectable with proper monitoring." } ] }, quiz: [ { q: "DNS cache poisoning injects false records into:", opts: ["A. The authoritative DNS server", "B. A caching resolver — all clients using it get wrong IP for the poisoned domain", "C. The client\'s browser", "D. The web server\'s DNS config"], answer: "B", explain: "DNS cache poisoning targets CACHING RESOLVERS (ISP DNS, corporate DNS) — not authoritative servers. Once poisoned, all clients using that resolver get the attacker\'s IP for the targeted domain. DNSSEC prevents this by cryptographically signing DNS records." }, { q: "SSL stripping works by:", opts: ["A. Exploiting weak SSL certificates", "B. Downgrading HTTPS to HTTP — user sends credentials in cleartext to the attacker", "C. Cracking SSL encryption keys", "D. Blocking SSL connections"], answer: "B", explain: "SSL stripping: attacker MITM position, intercepts HTTP. When user tries HTTPS, attacker relays HTTPS to server but presents HTTP to user. Credentials submitted on HTTP form go to attacker in cleartext. HSTS prevents this: browser remembers to ALWAYS use HTTPS, refuses HTTP." }, { q: "Kerberoasting extracts:", opts: ["A. NTLM hashes from LSASS memory", "B. Service tickets encrypted with service account password hashes for offline cracking", "C. User passwords from Active Directory", "D. Kerberos TGTs from the domain controller"], answer: "B", explain: "Kerberoasting: any authenticated domain user can request service tickets. These tickets are encrypted with the service account\'s NTLM hash. Extract with Rubeus/Impacket, crack offline with hashcat. Weak service account passwords fall in seconds to minutes." }, { q: "Golden Ticket attack requires:", opts: ["A. Physical access to domain controller", "B. The KRBTGT account\'s NTLM hash — allows forging valid Kerberos TGTs for any user", "C. Domain admin credentials only", "D. Compromising all domain controllers"], answer: "B", explain: "Golden Ticket: with KRBTGT hash, attacker can forge TGTs (Ticket Granting Tickets) for ANY user, including Domain Admins, with any privileges and any lifetime. Complete domain persistence. KRBTGT hash theft = full domain compromise. Detection: tickets with unusual attributes, offline ticket creation." }, { q: "Pass-the-Hash exploits:", opts: ["A. Weak password hash algorithms", "B. NTLM authentication accepting the password hash directly as proof — no password cracking needed", "C. Kerberos ticket forgery", "D. Certificate authentication"], answer: "B", explain: "NTLM challenge-response: client sends NTLM hash of password (not password itself). Attacker who captures the hash (via Mimikatz, Responder) can authenticate by sending the same hash. Password never needs to be cracked. Mitigation: disable NTLM, use Kerberos, Windows Credential Guard." }, { q: "SolarWinds supply chain attack was significant because:", opts: ["A. It used zero-day exploits", "B. Trusted software updates distributed backdoor to 18,000+ organisations — bypassing all perimeter controls", "C. It targeted only government systems", "D. It used ransomware"], answer: "B", explain: "SolarWinds: backdoor injected into ORION software BUILD process. Distributed via legitimate, SIGNED updates to 18,000+ customers. Every perimeter control trusted the signed update. 9+ months undetected. Lesson: supply chain trust must be verified; signed ≠ safe." }, { q: "HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) prevents:", opts: ["A. SSL certificate theft", "B. SSL stripping — browser refuses HTTP and always enforces HTTPS for the domain", "C. TLS downgrade to old versions", "D. Certificate spoofing"], answer: "B", explain: "HSTS: server sends Strict-Transport-Security header. Browser caches it and thereafter REFUSES HTTP for that domain — even if the attacker tries to strip to HTTP. First-visit problem: HSTS preloading (browser ships with list of HSTS domains) solves this." }, { q: "DNS tunnelling is hard to detect because:", opts: ["A. It uses encrypted DNS (DoH)", "B. DNS is commonly allowed through firewalls — encoded data in queries blends with legitimate traffic", "C. It uses port 443 which is always open", "D. It only works on internal networks"], answer: "B", explain: "DNS tunnelling: encode data in DNS query subdomains. Firewalls allow DNS (port 53) for name resolution. Requests look like DNS traffic. Detection requires: monitoring query length and entropy, high query volume per host, TXT record query frequency from endpoints." }, { q: "Session hijacking is prevented by the cookie attribute:", opts: ["A. Max-Age", "B. Secure and HttpOnly — Secure blocks HTTP transmission, HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access", "C. SameSite=None", "D. Domain=*"], answer: "B", explain: "Secure flag: cookie only sent over HTTPS — not transmitted on HTTP (no sniffing over insecure Wi-Fi). HttpOnly flag: JavaScript cannot access cookie — blocks XSS-based theft (document.cookie). Both are required for session cookie protection." }, { q: "Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) mitigate Kerberoasting because:", opts: ["A. gMSA accounts cannot be used for services", "B. gMSA passwords are 240-character random values auto-rotated by AD — computationally infeasible to crack", "C. gMSA accounts do not use Kerberos", "D. gMSA accounts are not registered in AD"], answer: "B", explain: "gMSA: AD automatically manages a 240-character random password, rotated on schedule. Even if an attacker captures the Kerberos service ticket and cracks it offline, the password rotates before the crack completes (typically every 30 days). No human sets or knows the password." } ] }, { id: "11-43", week: 11, day: 43, phase: "Security+", color: "#f472b6", title: "Security+ Targeted Review — High-Frequency Exam Topics", objective: "Drill the most tested Security+ topics: cryptography choices, access control models, attack identification, and protocol security.", messer: "Professor Messer SY0-701 — Full Review", notes: `## Cryptography Quick Reference\n\n**Symmetric:** AES (128/192/256), 3DES (legacy), DES (broken). Same key both sides. Fast. Bulk data.\n**Asymmetric:** RSA (2048/4096), ECC (256-521), DH/ECDH (key exchange). Key pair. Slow. Key exchange, signatures.\n**Hashing:** SHA-256/SHA-512 (current), MD5 (broken), bcrypt (passwords). One-way. Integrity, passwords.\n\n**When to use which:**\n- Encrypt bulk data: AES-256 (symmetric)\n- Exchange a key securely: ECDH/RSA (asymmetric)\n- Prove file integrity: SHA-256 (hash)\n- Store passwords: bcrypt/Argon2 (slow hash)\n- Sign a document: RSA or ECDSA (private key sign)\n- Verify signature: public key verify\n\n---\n\n## Authentication Quick Reference\n\n| Protocol | Use Case | Port |\n|----------|----------|------|\n| Kerberos | Windows AD authentication | 88 |\n| LDAP | Directory queries | 389 |\n| LDAPS | Encrypted directory | 636 |\n| RADIUS | Network access AAA | 1812/1813 |\n| TACACS+ | Device admin AAA | 49 |\n| SAML | Web SSO | HTTPS |\n| OAuth 2.0 | API authorisation | HTTPS |\n| OIDC | Web identity + auth | HTTPS |\n\n---\n\n## Access Control Models Summary\n\n- **DAC:** Owner controls access. Linux files, Windows NTFS.\n- **MAC:** System-enforced labels. Top Secret, Secret. Government/military.\n- **RBAC:** Role determines access. HR role, Developer role. Enterprise standard.\n- **ABAC:** Multiple attributes (user + resource + environment). Most granular.\n- **Rule-based:** ACLs, firewall rules.\n\n---\n\n## Attack Quick Identification\n\n| Attack | Key Identifier |\n|--------|----------------|\n| SQL injection | User input in SQL query: \' OR 1=1-- |\n| XSS | \`\n\n**Prevention:** Output encode all user-supplied data. CSP headers. HttpOnly cookie flag.\n\n---\n\n## Secure SDLC Integration\n\n**Shift left:** Move security earlier in development. Fix vulnerabilities when cheapest (design > code > test > prod).\n\n**SAST (Static Application Security Testing):**\n- Analyses source code without running it\n- Tools: SonarQube, Semgrep, Checkmarx, Bandit (Python)\n- Runs in CI pipeline on every commit\n- Finds: SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, buffer overflows\n\n**DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing):**\n- Tests running application by sending attack payloads\n- Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Nikto\n- Runs against staging environment\n- Finds: XSS, auth issues, injection vulnerabilities\n\n**SCA (Software Composition Analysis):**\n- Scans dependencies for known CVEs\n- Tools: Snyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check\n- Runs in CI on every build\n\n---\n\n## Security Headers\n\n\`\`\`http\nContent-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'\nX-Frame-Options: DENY\nX-Content-Type-Options: nosniff\nStrict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains\nReferrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin\n\`\`\``, exercise: { title: "Application Security Scenarios", instructions: "Apply OWASP and secure coding concepts.", items: [ "Identify the vulnerability: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='[userInput]' — and fix it.", "Stored XSS — how does it differ from reflected XSS in terms of impact?", "SSRF (A10) — what is the attack and why is it dangerous in cloud environments?", "SAST vs DAST — when to run each and what each finds.", "A developer hardcodes an API key in source code. What is the risk and fix?", "Content-Security-Policy header — what attack does it primarily mitigate?", "Broken Access Control (A01) — give an IDOR example and how to prevent it.", "Shift-left security — what does it mean and why does it save money?" ], answer: `1. SQL Injection (A03). Vulnerable: concatenating user input into SQL string — attacker sets userEmail = "' OR 1=1--" to return all users. Fix: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email=?", (userEmail,)) Parameterised queries: user input is NEVER interpreted as SQL. 2. Stored XSS: payload stored in the database (e.g. a forum post), served to EVERY user who views the page. One submission → all visitors affected. Reflected XSS: payload in URL, only affects users tricked into clicking the malicious link. Stored XSS has far broader impact — can affect all users of a platform, persist indefinitely, and steal session cookies at scale. 3. SSRF: Server-Side Request Forgery. Attacker tricks the server into making HTTP requests to internal resources. Example: image upload feature that fetches a URL — attacker submits http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS metadata service). Server fetches and returns cloud credentials. Dangerous in cloud: metadata endpoints expose IAM credentials, internal network services (Redis, Elasticsearch), and internal APIs not exposed externally. 4. SAST: run on every commit in CI pipeline — analyses source code. Finds: SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, unsafe functions, buffer overflows. No running app needed. DAST: run against staging environment — sends actual attack payloads. Finds: XSS, auth issues, real injection vulnerabilities at runtime. DAST confirms what SAST suspects. Use both: SAST for fast feedback, DAST for runtime validation. 5. Risk: (1) Source code often in version control (GitHub, GitLab) — key exposed to anyone with repo access. (2) Key appears in git history even after deletion. (3) Automated bots scan GitHub for API keys within seconds of commits. Fix: use environment variables or secrets management (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub Secrets). Rotate the key immediately. Use git-secrets or gitleaks pre-commit hook to prevent future commits. 6. CSP primarily mitigates XSS. Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' prevents inline scripts and scripts from external domains. Even if attacker injects , browser refuses to execute it because the script source isn't whitelisted. Also mitigates: clickjacking (frame-ancestors), data injection, mixed content. 7. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) example: GET /api/orders/12345 returns order data. Attacker changes 12345 to 12344 and gets another user's order. No authorisation check. Prevention: (1) Never use sequential/guessable IDs externally — use UUIDs. (2) Always verify the requesting user owns the resource: if order.user_id != current_user.id: return 403. 8. Shift-left: move security testing earlier in SDLC. Cost to fix a vulnerability: $1 in design, $10 in code, $100 in testing, $1000 in production (industry estimate). Catch SQL injection in code review: developer fixes in minutes.
